articleTitle: Grand Rotation Curve and Dark-Matter Halo in the Milky Way Galaxy
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: A grand rotation curve of the Milky Way Galaxy was constructed, which covers a wide range of radius from the Galactic Center to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 1 Mpc, and was deconvolved into bulge, disk, and halo components by least-squares fittings. We determined the masses and scale radii of the bulge and disk to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ {M_{\rm b}}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> (1.652 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.083) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{10}{\ M_\odot}$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ {a_{\rm b}}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0.522 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.037 kpc, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ {M_{\rm d}}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> (3.41 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.41) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{10}{\ M_\odot}$</tex>, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ {a_{\rm d}}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 3.19 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.35 kpc. The dark halo was fitted by the Navaro–Frenk–White (NFW) density profile, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \rho$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \rho_0/$</tex> [(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ R/h$</tex> )(1 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ R/h$</tex> )<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^2$</tex> ], and the fit yielded <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ h$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 12.5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.9 kpc and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \rho_0$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> (1.06 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.14) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-2}\ M_{\odot}$</tex> pc<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-3}$</tex> . The local dark-matter density near the Sun at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ R_0$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 8 kpc was estimated to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \rho_0^\odot$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> (6.12 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.80) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-3}\ M_{\odot}$</tex> pc<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-3}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0.235 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.030 GeV cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-3}$</tex> . The total mass inside the gravitational boundary of the Galaxy at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ R$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 385 kpc, a half distance to M 31, was estimated to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ {M_{\rm b+d+h}}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> (7.03 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 1.01) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{11}\ M_{\odot}$</tex> . This leads to a stellar baryon fraction of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ {M_{\rm b+d}}/{M_{\rm b+d+h}}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0.072 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.018. Considering the expected baryon fraction in the Local Group, we suggest that baryons in the form of hot gas are filling the dark halo with a temperature of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{6}$</tex> K and an emission measure of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-5}$</tex> pc cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{2}$</tex> . Such hot halo gas may share a small fraction of the observed X-ray background emission.

articleTitle: Superburst with Outburst from EXO 1745−248 in Terzan 5 with MAXI
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: MAXI/GSC detected a superburst from EXO 1745<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 248 in the globular cluster Terzan 5 on 2011 October 24. The GSC light curve shows an exponential decay with an <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ e$</tex>-folding time of 0.3 d. The spectra are consistent with the blackbody radiation, whose temperature is 2.2 keV and 1.2 keV at MJD 55858.56 and 55859.20, respectively. The fluence is 1.4 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{42}$</tex> erg in 2–20 keV, assuming an 8.7 kpc distance. The sphere radius of the blackbody and its luminosity are estimated to be 6.2 km and 1.1 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{38}$</tex> erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex>, respectively, from a spectral fitting at the flux peak. Those <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ e$</tex>-folding time, temperature, softening, fluence, and radius are typical of superbursts from low-mass X-ray binaries. The superburst was followed by an outburst 28 hours after the superburst onset. The outburst lasted for 5 d and the fluence was 4.3 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{42}$</tex> erg. The instability of the accretion disk caused by the superburst would be an explanation for the outburst, whereas the mass accretion of the matter evaporated from the surface of the companion star by the superburst would be another possibility.

articleTitle: Environmental Dependence of Stellar Mass, Star Formation Rate, Specific Star Formation Rate, and AGN Activity for an Apparent Magnitude Limited Main Galaxy Sample of the SDSS DR7
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In this study, we used an apparent magnitude limited Main galaxy sample of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 7 (SDSS DR7), and investigated the environmental dependence of stellar mass, the star formation rate (SFR), the specific star formation rate (SSFR, the star formation rate per unit stellar mass) and active galactic nucleus (AGN) activity. To decrease the Malmquist bias, we divided the whole apparent magnitude limited Main galaxy sample into many subsamples with a redshift binning size of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Delta{z}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0.01, and analysed the environmental dependence of these properties of subsamples in each redshift bin. It turns out that a strong environmental dependence of the stellar mass, SFR and SSFR could be observed in nearly all redshift bins of the apparent magnitude limited Main galaxy sample, and that in most redshift bins (except for a low redshift region of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0.02 to 0.06), the fraction of AGNs in the sample at low density apparently was larger than that in the sample at high density.

articleTitle: X-Ray Observations of the Supernova Remnant W 28 with Suzaku. I. Spectral Study of the Recombining Plasma
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present Suzaku results of the mixed-morphology supernova remnant W 28. The X-ray spectra of the central region of W 28 exhibit many bright emission lines from highly ionized atoms. An optically thin thermal plasma in collisional ionization equilibrium, either of single temperature or multi temperatures, failed to reproduce the data with line-like and bump-like residuals at the Si-Ly<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha$</tex> energy and at 2.4–5.0 keV, respectively. The bumps probably correspond to radiative recombination continua from He-like Si and S. A simple recombining plasma model nicely fit the bump structures, but failed to fit low-energy bands. The overall spectra can be fit with a multi–ionization-temperature plasma with a common electron temperature. The multi-ionization temperatures are interpreted as elemental differences of ionization and recombination timescales. These results prefer the rarefaction scenario for the origin of the recombining plasma.

articleTitle: V524 Monocerotis: A Marginal Contact Binary with a Cyclic Period Variation
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have secured and analyzed three-color light curves of V524 Monocerotis with the 2003 version of the Wilson–Devinney code. We confirmed that V524 Mon is a shallow W-type contact binary system with a mass ratio of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$q$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 2.099 and a degree of contact factor of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$f$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 7.7%. Based on the new eight times of the light minima and those published by previous investigators, we find that the orbital period of the binary shows a long-term decrease (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$dp/dt$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>1.52 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-10}$</tex>), while it undergoes a cyclic oscillation (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{3}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 23.93 yr, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A_{3}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 0.0082 d). The long-term period decrease can be explained by mass transfer from the primary to the secondary. The cyclic change, explained as the light-travel time effect, reveals the presence of a tertiary companion. The marginal contact configuration and the continuous period decrease both suggest that the system may be a newly formed contact binary.

articleTitle: Low-Resolution Spectroscopy of the Recurrent Nova T Pyxidis at its Early Stage of the 2011 Outburst
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present our observational results of the recurrent nova T Pyx at its early stage of the 2011 outburst, using a low-resolution spectrograph (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ R$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \approx$</tex> 400) attached to a 28 cm telescope. The total number of nights of our observation was 11, among which 9 nights were during the pre-maximum stage. As a result, we obtained a detailed evolutional feature of this recurrent nova on the way to its maximum light. At first, on the earliest three nights (25–21 days before maximum), broad and prominent emission lines, such as Balmer series, He I, He II, N II, N III, and O I together with the P Cyg profile, are seen on the spectra. The blueshifted absorption minima of H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha$</tex> yields a maximum expansion velocity of approximately 2200 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex>, and the velocity gradually decreases. Then, helium and nitrogen lines are weakened day by day. After that (18 days before maximum light), Fe II (multiplets) lines emerge on the spectra. These lines are then strengthened day by day, and the P Cyg profiles also become more prominent. Accordingly, the expansion velocities turn to gradual increase. In addition, during the pre-maximum stage, the nova spectral type of T Pyx is thought to evolve from the He<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ /$</tex> N type to the Fe II one.

articleTitle: Video Observation of the Leonids 2001 Activity
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: This paper presents an analysis of records obtained by video equipment of the 2001 Leonid meteor storm. Totally, 3712 meteors, including 22 non-Leonid ones, were recognized from the record of 247 min. The brightness of meteors was measured with the software “LIMovie”, and a population index of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 2.01<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \pm\ $</tex>0.05 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>8 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\le$</tex> mag <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\le$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>3) was thus derived. We proposed a way to derive the mass-distribution index, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$s$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 1.82, from only our one-station data. The maximum of the activity appeared at 18<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm h}$</tex>25<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm m}$</tex> UT with an effective peak of ZHR<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{90^{\circ}\times67^{\circ}}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 52606 (mag <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\le$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>6.5). There are also compatible sub-peaks and high plateaus beside the main peak. One of them may correspond to the predicted 9-revolution dust trail (ejection in 1699). In this article we treat the cross section of the influx zone as a trapezoid. The peak “influx rate” generated by the 4-revolution dust trail (ejection in 1866) thus derived would be 6.76 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-5}\ $</tex>km<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}\ $</tex>s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> (mag <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\le$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>6.5), and the corresponding “spatial number density” would be 9.52 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-7}\ $</tex>km<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex> (mag <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\le$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>6.5).

articleTitle: New Photometric Investigation of the G-Type Contact Binary GSC 0763-0572
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present new CCD photometric light curves of the W UMa-type binary system GSC 0763-0572 in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ R$</tex>, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ I$</tex> bands. Here, the light curves in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ R$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ I$</tex> bands are the first to be obtained. The primary component of this system belongs to a G-type solar-like star; our new observation indicates that the activities of GSC 0763-0572 may be stable. Based on all available times of the light minimum, we found that the orbital period is variable. The <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ O$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ C$</tex> curve suggested that the period of GSC 0763-0572 is undergoing a continuous increase at a rate of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ dP/dt$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 5.81(33) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-7}$</tex> d yr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> . Photometric solutions were derived by using the Wilson–Devinney code. We confirmed that this system is A-subtype overcontact binary with a degree of contact factor of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ f$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 31.0% (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 1.5%), a mass ratio of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ q$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0.2330, and a temperature difference of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Delta{T}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 31 K. The long-term increase of the orbital period can be explained by mass transfer from the less-massive component to the more-massive one. It's inferred that GSC 0763-0572 may presently be in an expanding state of thermal relaxation oscillation, and may finally evolve into a rapid-rotating single star.

articleTitle: Early Evolution of Spherical Ejecta Expanding into the Circumstellar Matter at Ultra-Relativistic Speeds
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present a new self-similar solution describing the early evolution of an ultra-relativistic flow resulting from a collision of homologously expanding spherical ejecta with the circumstellar matter, in which a shock wave propagates in the circumstellar matter, while a weak discontinuity propagates in the ejecta at the sound speed.

articleTitle: The Jet-Disk Symbiosis in Blazar and Unified Model of FSRQs and BL Lac Objects
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Using multi-wave band data for a large sample of 70 blazars, including 38 flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs) and 32 BL Lac Objeces, we studied the correlations for both the flux and luminosity of the broad-line emission (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$F_{\rm BLR}$</tex>) with the near-infrared flux (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$F_{K}$</tex>), X-ray flux (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$F_{X}$</tex>) and radio flux at 5 GHz (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$F_{R}$</tex>), respectively. We could see that there is always a strong correlation between the broad-line and multi-wave bands for a sample of 70 blazars; also, the slopes of the corresponding linear-regression equations are close to 1, which is consistent with the theoretical results. These results provide some new experimental evidence about coupling of the accretion disk and the jet of blazars. Simultaneously, we also indicated that the relative location of BL Lacs and FSRQs are quite separated, and that the luminosity of the the broad-line emission for BL Lacs is much less for FSRQs, which can prove that FSRQs and BL Lacs could be considered as a single population, or FSRQs and BL Lacs should be regarded as a class. But they are in different evolutionary stages of blazars, and have different types of accretion disks with different line-to-continuum ratios. Finally, the unified model of FSRQs and BL Lacs is also discussed.

articleTitle: Low-Resolution Spectroscopy of Hot Post-AGB Candidates II. LS, LSS, LSE Stars and Additional IRAS Sources
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Hot (OB) post-asymptotic giant branch (post-AGB) stars are immediate progenitors of planetary nebulae (PNe). Very few hot post-AGB stars are known. Detecting new hot post-AGB candidates and follow-up multiwavelength studies will enable us to further understand the processes during the post-AGB evolution that lead to the formation of PNe. Case-Hamburg OB star surveys and their extension (LS, LSS, and LSE catalogues) and IRAS (point source) catalogues are good sources for detecting new hot post-AGB candidates from low-resolution spectroscopy. Spectral types are determined from low-resolution optical spectra of 44 stars selected from the LS, LSS, and LSE catalogues. Unlike the stars mentioned in the first paper, the stars discussed in this paper were selected using criteria other than positional coincidence with an IRAS source with far-IR (IRAS) colours similar to post-AGB supergiants and planetary nebulae. These included high galactic latitude, spectral types of O, B, A supergiants, emission lines in the spectrum and known spectral peculiarity. From the present study we find that LSS 1179, LSS 1222, LSS 1256, LSS 1276, LSS 1341, LSS 1394, LSS 2241, LSS 2429, LSS 4560, LSE 3, LSE 16, LSE 42, and LSE 67 to be new hot post-AGB candidates. Further studies of these candidates are needed.

articleTitle: Observational Report on the Classical Nova KT Eridani
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: A report is presented on spectroscopic and multi-color photometric observations of the high Galactic latitude classical nova KT Eridani (Nova Eridani 2009). After 12.2 d from maximum light, broad and prominent emission lines of the Balmer series, Hei, Heii, Nii, Niii, and Oi can be seen on the spectra. The FWHM of the H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\alpha}$</tex> line yields an expansion velocity of approximately 3400 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. After 279.4 d from maximum light, we can see prominent emission lines of Heii and [Oiii] on the spectrum. Among them, [Oiii] (4959, 5007) lines show multiple peaks. From the obtained light curve, KT Eri is classified to be a very fast nova, with a decline rate by two magnitudes of 6.2 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex> 0.3 d and three of 14.3 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex> 0.7 d. We tried to estimate the absolute magnitude (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_V$</tex>) using the Maximum Magnitude versus Rate of Decline relationship and distance of KT Eri. The calculated <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_V$</tex> is approximately <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>9. Accordingly, the distance and Galactic height are approximately 7 kpc and 4 kpc, respectively. Hence, KT Eri is concluded to be located outside of the Galactic disk.

articleTitle: Discovery of Superhumps during a Normal Outburst of SU Ursae Majoris
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on time-resolved photometry during a 2012 January normal outburst of SU UMa. The light curve shows hump-like modulations with a period of 0.07903(11) d, which coincides with the known superhump period of SU UMa during superoutbursts. We interpret this as a superhump, based on the observed periodicity, profiles of the averaged light curve, and the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$g'$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$I_{\rm c}$</tex> variation during the normal outburst. This is the first case that superhumps have been detected during an isolated normal outburst of SU UMa-type dwarf novae. The present result strongly suggests that the radius of the accretion disk already reaches the 3:1 resonance, even in the midst of the supercycle.

articleTitle: Brightness of HAYABUSA Spacecraft Reentry: Artificial Fireball
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: During reentry of the HAYABUSA spacecraft, the main body became a bright fireball of full-moon class. While the images were being taken by a team of ground-based observations, it was too bright to saturate the detectors in most of our instruments. In order to estimate the brightness quantitatively, we utilized ghost images of the main body together with the spectral data. We managed to estimate the time variation of the brightness, which had several peaks of flare ups possibly due to a rapid increase of the total cross section of the fragments. The maximum brightness obtained was <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>13.1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \pm\ $</tex>0.1, the apparent magnitude at 13<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm h}$</tex>52<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm m}$</tex>19<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$.\!\!\!^{\rm s}$</tex>8 UT, which corresponds to a height of 57.2 km above sea level. The corresponding absolute magnitude is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>13.7<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \pm\ $</tex>0.1.

articleTitle: On the Error Reduction of a Simple Symplectic Integrator
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: An analysis of truncation errors of the simplest symplectic integrator is revisited. We performed an analytical error estimate of this integrator within the framework of a canonical perturbation method, taking the two-body system as an example. Our study was motivated by the desire to remove any confusion in the derivation of this issue in one standard literature along this line of research. We repeated the derivation, and examined how a secular numerical error arises in symplectic integration. We showed that it is possible to substantially eliminate a secular numerical error by choosing appropriate initial conditions, as previous studies have shown. On the other hand, depending on boundary parameter values, such as the eccentricity in the two-body system, we could see that it is sometimes impossible to reduce the secular numerical error by changing the starting conditions. We also numerically demonstrated this reduction, or lack of reduction of numerical errors by taking a restricted three-body system as an example. We confirmed that the so-called “iterative start” of symplectic integrators works in certain systems.

articleTitle: FIBRE-Pac: FMOS Image-Based Reduction Package
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The FIBRE-pac (FMOS image-based reduction package) is an IRAF-based reduction tool for the fiber multiple-object spectrograph (FMOS) of the Subaru telescope. To reduce FMOS images, a number of special techniques are necessary, because each image contains about 200 separate spectra with airglow emission lines variable in spatial and time domains, and with complicated throughput patterns for airglow masks. In spite of these features, almost all of the reduction processes, except for a few steps, are carried out automatically by scripts in text format, making it easy to check the commands step by step. Wavelength- and flux-calibrated images together with their noise maps are obtained using this reduction package.

articleTitle: Period Analysis using the Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (Lasso)
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We introduced least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (Lasso) in obtaining periodic signals in unevenly spaced time-series data. A very simple formulation with the combination of a large set of sine and cosine functions has been shown to yield a very robust estimate; also, the peaks in the resultant power spectra were very sharp. We studied the response of Lasso to low signal-to-noise data, asymmetric signals and very closely separated multiple signals. When the length of the observation was sufficiently long, all of them were not serious obstacles to Lasso. We analyzed the 100-year visual observations of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \delta $</tex> Cep, and obtained a very accurate period of 5.366326(16) d. The error in the period estimation was several times smaller than in the phase dispersion minimization. We also modeled the historical data of R Sct, and obtained a reasonable fit to the data. The model, however, lost its predictive ability after the end of the interval used for modeling, which is probably a result of the chaotic nature of the pulsations of this star. We also provided a sample R code for making this analysis.

articleTitle: Self-Charge-Filling (SCF) Effect of Suzaku XIS
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We demonstrate the importance of the self-charge-filling (SCF) effect for the analysis of bright and line-rich sources with the Suzaku X-ray imaging spectrometer (XIS) if spaced-row charge injection (SCI) is not applied. The SCF-effect changes the central energy of lines depending on the extracted region or the event densities of the images. We propose a correction method of the SCF-effect and show its validity by applying it to the extraction of the spectra of Cygnus X-3.

Author Keywords: X-rays: CCD: Charge Injection: Suzaku satellite

articleTitle: Initial Results from Nobeyama Molecular Gas Observations of Distant Bright Galaxies
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present initial results from the CO survey toward high-redshift galaxies using the Nobeyama 45 m telescope. Using a new wide bandwidth spectrometer equipped with a two-beam SIS receiver, we have obtained three new detections of high-redshift (z<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 1.6–3.4) submillimeter galaxies (SXDF 1100.001/HXMM02, SDP9, and SDP17), one tentative detection (SDSS J160705<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>533558), and one non-detection (COSMOS-AzTEC1). The galaxies observed during the commissioning phase are sources with known spectroscopic redshifts from previous optical or wide-band submillimeter spectroscopy. The derived molecular gas mass and line widths from Gaussian fits are <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{11}\ M_{\odot}$</tex> and 430–530 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, respectively, which are consistent with previous CO observations of distant submillimeter galaxies and quasars. The spectrometer, which realizes a maximum of 32 GHz instantaneous bandwidth, will provide new science capabilities at the Nobeyama 45 m telescope, allowing us to determine redshifts of bright submillimeter selected galaxies without any prior redshift information.

articleTitle: Bursting Activity in a High-Mass Star-Forming Region G33.640.21 Observed with the 6.7 GHz Methanol Maser
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on the detection of bursts of 6.7 GHz methanol maser emission in a high-mass star-forming region, G33.64<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>0.21. One of the spectral components of the maser in this source changed its flux density by 7 times that of the previous day, and it decayed with a timescale of 5 days. The burst occurred repeatedly in the spectral component, and no other components showed such variability. A VLBI observation with the Japanese VLBI Network (JVN) showed that the burst location was at the southwest edge of a spatial distribution, and the bursting phenomenon occurred in a region much smaller than 70 AU. We suggest an impulsive energy release, like a stellar flare, as a possible mechanism for the burst. These results imply that 6.7 GHz methanol masers could be a useful new probe for studying bursting activity in the process of the star formation of high-mass YSOs with a high-resolution of AU scale.

articleTitle: Observed Magnitude and Luminous Efficiency of Reentry Capsule of HAYABUSA Spacecraft
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The brightness variation of the sample capsule of the HAYABUSA spacecraft was observed during reentry into Earth's atmosphere on 2010 June 13 UT. The capsule was observed from 13<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm h}$</tex>52<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm m}$</tex>01<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm s}$</tex> through 13<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm h}$</tex>52<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm m}$</tex>38<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm s}$</tex> UT, with three peaks of brightness between 13<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm h}$</tex>52<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm m}$</tex>19<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm s}$</tex> and 21<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm s}$</tex> UT. The absolute magnitude of the highest peak was <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>5.7(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.9) at 13<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm h}$</tex>52<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm m}$</tex>18<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$.\hskip-1mm^{\rm s}$</tex>6 UT. The luminous efficiency reached to the largest value of 0.89% (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>1.14%, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>0.50%) at a time corresponding to an altitude of 58.1 km above sea level.

articleTitle: High-Resolution Near-Infrared Polarimetry of a Circumstellar Disk around UX Tau A
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ H$</tex>-band polarimetric imagery of UX Tau A taken with HiCIAO/AO188 on the Subaru Telescope. UX Tau A has been classified as a pre-transitional disk object, with a gap structure separating its inner and outer disks. Our imagery taken with the 0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \rlap{\hskip1pt .}''$</tex> 15 (21 AU) radius coronagraphic mask has revealed a strongly polarized circumstellar disk surrounding UX Tau A, which extends to 120 AU, at a spatial resolution of 0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \rlap{\hskip1pt .}''$</tex> 1 (14 AU). It is inclined by 46<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{\circ}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{\circ}$</tex>, since the west side is nearest. Although SED modeling and sub-millimeter imagery have suggested the presence of a gap in the disk, with the inner edge of the outer disk estimated to be located at 25–30 AU, we detect no evidence of a gap at the limit of our inner working angle (23 AU) at the near-infrared wavelength. We attribute the observed strong polarization (up to 66%) to light scattering by dust grains in the disk. However, neither polarization models of the circumstellar disk based on Rayleigh-scattering nor Mie-scattering approximations were consistent with the observed azimuthal profile of the polarization degrees of the disk. Instead, a geometric optics model of the disk with nonspherical grains with radii of 30 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \mu$</tex> m is consistent with the observed profile. We suggest that the dust grains have experienced frequent collisional coagulations, and have grown in the circumstellar disk of UX Tau A.

articleTitle: Turbulence Effects on Bremsstrahlung Emission in the Turbulent Solar Plasma
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Turbulence effects on bremsstrahlung emission due to the electron–ion interaction were investigated in the turbulent solar plasma. The effective interaction potential, taking into account the correction factor to the nonlinear dielectric function due to plasma turbulence, and the impact-parameter method were employed in order to obtain the bremsstrahlung radiation cross section in a turbulent plasma as a function of the impact parameter, diffusion coefficient, radiation photon energy, projectile energy, and plasma parameters. It has been shown that the turbulence effects considerably enhance the bremsstrahlung radiation cross section. In addition, it was found that the turbulence effects of the solar atmosphere on the bremsstrahlung cross section increase with increasing radiation photon energy, but decrease with increasing thermal energy. It can be expected that the Landau damping effect on the bremsstrahlung spectrum from the solar corona is less important than that from the solar chromospheres due to temperature jumps. However, the effect of the plasma turbulence on the bremsstrahlung spectrum from the solar chromosphere would be smaller than that from the solar corona.

articleTitle: Subaru Constraint on Circular Polarization in I-Band Emission from the Magnetar 4U 0142+61
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the first imaging circular polarimetry of the anomalous X-ray pulsar (AXP) 4U 0142<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>61 at optical wavelengths. The AXP is the only magnetar that has been well studied at optical and infrared wavelengths, and is known to have a complicated broad-band spectrum over the wavelength range. The optical polarimetric observation was carried out with the 8.2-m Subaru telescope at the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$I$</tex>-band. From the observation, the degree of circular polarization, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V$</tex>, was measured to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 1.1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm $</tex>2.0%, or <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\vert V\vert$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\leq$</tex> 4.3% (90% confidence). The relatively large uncertainty was due to the faintness of the source (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$I$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 23.4–24.0). Considering the currently suggested models for optical emission from magnetars, our result is not sufficiently conclusive to discriminate the models. We suggest that because linear polarization is expected to be strong in the models, linear polarimetry of this magnetar should be conducted.

articleTitle: Slow-Scan Observations with the Infrared Camera (IRC) aboard AKARI
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the characterization and calibration of the slow-scan observation mode of the Infrared Camera (IRC) aboard AKARI. The IRC Slow-scan observations were operated at the S9W (9 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \mu$</tex> m) and L18W (18 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \mu$</tex> m) bands. We developed a toolkit for data reduction of the IRC Slow-scan observations. We introduced a ``self-pointing reconstruction'' method to improve the positional accuracy to as good as 1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \overset{''}{.}$</tex> . The sizes of the point spread functions were derived to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 6<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \overset{''}{.}$</tex> at the S9W band and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 7<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \overset{''}{.}$</tex> at the L18W bands in full width at half maximum. Flux calibrations were achieved with observations of 3 and 4 infrared standard stars at the S9W and L18W bands, respectively. The flux uncertainties are estimated to be better than 20% from comparisons with the AKARI IRC PSC and the WISE preliminary catalog.

articleTitle: Radiative Transfer in Anisotropic Scattering Media
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Transfer and moment equations in anisotropic scattering media are formulated under a simple linear model using the Eddington approximation. In the transfer equation, a term including the radiative flux appears, and the first moment equation is also modified, while the zeroth moment equation does not change, since the scattering processes exchange momentum, but not energy. Moment equations and transfer equation are solved for several simple cases to clarify the qualitative properties of radiative transfer in anisotropic scattering media. When forward scattering dominates, the radiative intensity is enhanced in some cases, while the gradient of the mean intensity decreases in other cases, depending on the boundary conditions for the problem. These analytic expressions are helpful in studying and understanding the radiative properties of stars with dusty envelopes, interstellar matter, protoplanetary disks and star forming regions, and the dusty universe.

articleTitle: Do Environmental Conditions Affect the Dust-Induced Fragmentation in Low-Metallicity Clouds? Effect of Pre-Ionization and Far-Ultraviolet/Cosmic-Ray Fields
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We study the effects of the fully ionized initial state, or pre-ionization, on the subsequent thermal evolution of low-metallicity clouds under various intensities of external far-ultraviolet (FUV) and cosmic-ray (CR) fields. Pre-ionization significantly affects the thermal and dynamical evolution of metal-free clouds without FUV/CRs by way of efficient HD formation. On the other hand, the pre-ionization effect on thermal evolution is limited in the very low-density regime for more metal-enriched clouds ([Z<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ /$</tex> H] <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ >rsim$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 4), or those under a modest FUV (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ >rsim$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-3}$</tex> ) field or CR field (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ >rsim$</tex> 0.1) of the present-day galactic disk levels. In any case, for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ >rsim$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{8}$</tex> cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-3}$</tex>, neither the initial ionization state nor the irradiating FUV strength affect the thermal evolution. The dust cooling is an important mechanism for making sub-solar mass fragments in low-metallicity gas. Since this fragmentation occurs at the temperature minimum by dust cooling at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ >rsim$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{10}$</tex> cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-3}$</tex>, this process is not vulnerable either to the initial ionization state or external radiation.

articleTitle: Asymmetric Dust Jets and Extended Structure of 22P/Kopff Observed During 2009 Appearance
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: 22P/Kopff images were taken with Multicolor Imaging Telescopes for Survey and Monstrous Explosions (MITSuME) 3ch simultaneous CCD cameras on the Ishigakijima astronomical observatory 105-cm telescope and a 2kCCD camera on the Kiso 105-cm Schmidt telescope from 2009 August to December after the passage of its perihelion on 2009 May 25. We confirmed that the near-nuclear fan-shaped jet structure extended toward the south. Whereas we detected a dust trail structure on the project orbit of the parent nucleus, we could not confirm the obvious neck-line structure. We deduced a pole orientation of (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha_{\rm pl}$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \delta_{\rm pl}$</tex> ) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> (302<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 30, 62<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 10) or (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha_{\rm pl}$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \delta_{\rm pl}$</tex> ) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> (122<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 30, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 62 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 10) in the case of prograde or retrograde rotation, based on the fan-shaped jet. In addition, we conducted a model simulation of the dust orbital evolution, and found that the observed dust morphology of the fan-shaped jet and dust trail can well explain the dust emission near the south polar region. Finally, we conclude that the surface of 22P/Kopff is becoming largely dormant, but the polar region is still active, as we saw in the Deep Space 1 image of 19P/Borrelly.

articleTitle: An Accretion-Disk Model with Cooling through Molecular Lines
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan

The abundances of molecules were calculated numerically by the chemical reaction network, along with the structure of the disk. It was found that, when the model is applied to the Keplerian disk observed in the nucleus of NGC 4258, the temperature is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ T$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \simeq$</tex> 400–500 K, the number density of molecular hydrogen is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ n$</tex> (H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" of H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ _2$</tex> O amounts to 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-3}$</tex> in the maser emitting region for the mass-accretion rate <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \dot{M}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \simeq$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-7}\ M_{\odot }$</tex> yr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> and the viscosity parameter <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0.1. In the outer region, the disk is both geometrically and optically thin, the drift time is at most 1 Gyr, self-gravity of the disk can be neglected, and irradiation from the inner disk is of also a negligible effect. The Toomre <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ Q$</tex> parameter is greater than unity, leading the disk to be gravitationally stable. It was also found that these physical circumstances cannot be achieved in the optically thick model cooled by blackbody radiation.

articleTitle: OAO/ISLE Near-IR Spectroscopy of IRAS Galaxies
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the results of the near-infrared (IR) spectroscopy of nine IRAS galaxies (NGC 1266, NGC 1320, NGC 2633, NGC 2903, NGC 3034, Mrk 33, NGC 7331, NGC 7625, NGC 7714) with the ISLE imager and spectrograph mounted on the Okayama Astrophysical Observatory 1.88-m telescope. [Fe II] 1.257<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \mu$</tex>m and Pa<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex> emission lines were observed for the whole sample, while H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex> 2.121<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \mu$</tex>m and Br<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex> lines were additionally obtained for two sources, whose flux ratios were used as a diagnostic tool of dominant energy sources of the galaxies. We found that the nucleus of NGC 1266 is most likely a low-ionization nuclear emission-line region (LINER), while NGC 2633 and NGC 2903 possibly harbor active galactic nuclei (AGNs). No AGN or LINER signal is found for other objects. In addition, we found the spectral features, which are indicative of some unusual phenomena occurring in the galaxies, such as the large [Fe II] line widths compared to the local escape velocity in NGC 1266. The present work shows the potential ability of ISLE to shed new light on the nature of infrared galaxies, either through a statistical survey of galaxies or an exploration of spectral features found in individual objects.

Author Keywords: galaxies: individual (NGC 1266, NGC 1320, NGC 2633, NGC 2903, NGC 3034, Mrk 33, NGC 7331, NGC 7625, NGC 7714)

articleTitle: Alpha-Viscosity Effects in Slender Tori
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We explore effects of the Shakura–Sunyaev <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha$</tex>-viscosity on the dynamics and oscillations of slender tori. We start with a slow secular evolution of the torus. We show that the angular-momentum profile approaches the Keplerian one on a timescale longer than a dynamical one by a factor on the order of 1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ / \alpha$</tex> . We then focus our attention on the oscillations of the torus. We discuss the effects of various angular-momentum distributions. Using a perturbation theory, we have found a rather general result that the high-order acoustic modes are damped by the viscosity, while the high-order inertial modes are enhanced. We calculate viscous growth rates for the lowest-order modes, and show that already the lowest-order inertial mode is unstable for less-steep angular-momentum profiles, or very close to the central gravitating object.

articleTitle: New Period Investigation of Near Contact Binary BF Virginis
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The near contact binary BF Virginis was monitored by us from 2007 to 2011 with the 60-cm telescope of Yunnan Observatory. Eight new observed times of light minimum were derived. All of the available eclipse times, spanning more than 100 yr, were analyzed. It is found that there exists a cyclic variation with a semi-amplitude of 0.034 d and a period of 63.3 yr, superposed by an upward parabolic variation. The upward parabolic change can be explained as a continuous period increase due to mass transfer from the secondary to the primary component of BF Vir, which supports the secondary filling near contact configuration. The period oscillation can be explained either by the light-time effect due to the presence of a third body or by magnetic activity. If it is caused by the light-time effect, the minimum mass and the corresponding orbital radius of the additional body should be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ m_{3}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0.93 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ M_{\odot}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ a_{3}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 19.4 AU, respectively. On the other hand, the period oscillation may be explained as a consequence of magnetic cycles in its secondary component. In this case, the required variation of the quadrupole moment is calculated to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Delta{Q}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 2.1 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{50}$</tex> g cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^2$</tex> .

articleTitle: Evolution of Supernova Remnants Expanding out of the Dense Circumstellar Matter into the Rarefied Interstellar Medium
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We carried out 3D-hydrodynamical calculations for the interaction of expanding supernova ejecta with the dense circumstellar matter (CSM) and the rarefied interstellar medium (ISM) outside. The CSM is composed of stellar-wind matter from the progenitor in its pre-supernova phase, and assumed to be axially symmetric: more matter around the equator than in the polar direction driven by rotation of the progenitor. Because of the high density of the CSM, the ionization state of the shock-heated ejecta quickly becomes equilibrium with the electron temperature. When the blast wave breaks out of the CSM into the rarefied ISM, the shocked ejecta cools rapidly due to adiabatic expansion, and hence an over-ionized/recombining plasma would be left. The ejecta is reheated by the second reverse shock due to the interaction with the ISM. We calculated the emission measure of the supernova remnant (SNR) along the line of sight, and found that the over-ionized plasma appears to be bar-like with wings in the edge-on (equatorial view), while shell-like in the face-on (polar view) geometry with respect to the rotation axis. Hot gas heated by the blast wave exists in the outermost region of the SNR with a nearly complete shell, but the X-rays therefrom are too faint to be observable. Thus, depending on the viewing angle, the SNR of the over-ionized plasma would exhibit a center-filled morphology in X-rays, like W 49 B, a mixed-morphology SNR. The bar-like structure is swept out by the second reverse shock and disappears eventually, and then the SNR becomes shell-like in both the equatorial and polar views in the later phase of evolution.

articleTitle: Maser Emission toward the Infrared Dark Cloud G359.94+0.17 Seen in Silhouette against the Galactic Center
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The infrared dark cloud G359.94<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>0.17 is a conspicuous, opaque cloud, which is seen in silhouette against the Galactic center. We found unexpectedly strong (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>50 Jy) maser emission of CH<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_3$</tex>OH at 44 GHz with additional weak 22 GHz H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>O maser and 43 GHz SiO thermal emissions toward this cloud. Detections of these molecular lines indicate that strong star-forming activities are proceeding in this cloud, which was not reported previously despite of numerous studies toward the Galactic center. The line profiles of the NH<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_3$</tex> inversion lines at 23 GHz indicate that G359.94<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>0.17 is composed of mainly two clouds with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V_{\rm lsr}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 0, and 15 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> overlapped on the line of sight. The maser emission is associated with the 15 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> cloud, suggesting that it is located at the Norma spiral arm.

articleTitle: The Active Contact Binary FU Draconis: Four Color Light Curves and Period Changes
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Secured four color light curves of FU Dra were analyzed with the 2003 version of the Wilson and Devinney (WD) code. It was shown that FU Dra is still a W-type contact binary system, but might have a high fill-out factor (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$f$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 26.7% <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex> 1.0%). A dark spot was introduced on the massive cool component. A period investigation based on all available data shows that the period of the system may include a long-term increase (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$dP/dt$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 8.8 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex> 2.9 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-8}$</tex> d yr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>) and an oscillation (semi-amplitude of 0.0024 d, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$P_3$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 7.8 yr). The long-term period decrease may be caused by mass transfer, though the periodic oscillation may be rooted in cyclic magnetic activity.

articleTitle: Near-Infrared Survey of Bright Rimmed Clouds
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We conducted wide-field near-infrared imaging observations of 32 bright rimmed clouds (BRCs). Given a detection limit of 17.7 mag at the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ K$</tex>-band, we identified 2099 objects as young stellar object (YSO) candidates that displayed near-infrared excesses. Their masses, estimated from luminosities, range from 0.006 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ M_{\odot}$</tex> to 2.7 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ M_{\odot}$</tex> . The candidates are not uniformly distributed. For 21 BRCs, more than half of the associated YSO candidates are located inside the cloud. We found clear evidence of triggered star formation. The number of YSO candidates is not correlated with the core mass of the molecular clouds. Instead, the YSO number increases with increasing UV photon flux from the exciting star illuminating the cloud surface. UV radiation activates star formation in the BRCs.

articleTitle: Variation of Meteor Heights and Solar-Cycle Activity
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Photographic meteor observations of the Perseid meteoroid stream compiled from the IAU Meteor Data Center catalogue are analyzed from the viewpoint of possible long-term variation of meteor heights with the solar-cycle activity, which was previously reported from radio observations. The observed beginning and end-point heights of the Perseids, normalized for the geocentric velocity and the absolute photographic magnitude, do not show a variation consistent with the solar-cycle activity. This result is valid for the mass range of larger meteoroids observed by photographic techniques, and must be still verified also for the range of smaller meteoroids observed by TV and radio methods.

articleTitle: Molecular and Atomic Gas toward HESS J1745−303 in the Galactic Center: Further Support for the Hadronic Scenario
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We compared TeV <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>-rays with new <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$l$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$b$</tex>) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> (358<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ\!\!\!.$</tex>9, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ\!\!\!.$</tex>5) at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V_\mathrm{LSR}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>100–0 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> shows a reasonable positional agreement with the primary peak (northern part) of the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>-ray source. For the southern part of HESS J1745<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>303, we have seen no CO counterpart, whereas H I gas in the SGPS H I dataset shows a possible counterpart to the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>-ray source. This H I gas may be optically thick, as supported by the H I line shape similar to the optically thick <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO. We estimate the total mass of interstellar protons including both the molecular and atomic gas to be 2 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{6}M\odot$</tex> and the cosmic-ray proton energy to be 6 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{48}\ $</tex>erg in the hadronic scenario. We discuss possible origins of the cosmic-ray protons including the nearby SNR G359.1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>0.5. The SNR may be able to explain the northern <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>-ray source, but the southern source seems to be too far to be energized by the SNR. As an alternative, we argue that the second-order Fermi acceleration in the inter-clump space surrounded by randomly moving high-velocity clumps may offer a possible mechanism to accelerate protons across the entire HESS source. The large turbulent motion with a velocity dispersion of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>15 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> has an energy density two orders of magnitude higher than in the solar vicinity, and is viable as the energy source.

articleTitle: Pilot VLBI Survey of SiO v = 3 J = 1 → 0 Maser Emission around Evolved Stars
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In this letter, we report on detections of SiO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ v$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 3 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ J$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \rightarrow$</tex> 0 maser emission in very long-baseline interferometric (VLBI) observations towards 4 out of 12 long-period variable stars: WX Psc, R Leo, W Hya, and T Cep. The detections towards WX Psc and T Cep are new ones. We also present successful astrometric observations of SiO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ v$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 2 and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ v$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 3 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ J$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \rightarrow$</tex> 0 maser emissions associated with two stars: WX Psc and W Hya and their position-reference continuum sources: J010746.0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 131205 and J135146.8<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 291218 with the VLBI Exploration of Radio Astrometry (VERA). The relative coordinates of the position-reference continuum source and SiO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ v$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 3 maser spots were measured with respect to those of an SiO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ v$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 2 maser spot adopted as a fringe-phase reference. Thus, the faint continuum sources were inversely phase-referenced to the bright maser sources. This implies possible registration of multiple SiO maser line maps onto a common coordinate system with 10 microarcsecond-level accuracy.
