(2010, PASJ, 62, 613), we have found that the present sample tends to give a flatter distribution to the shortest period and a shorter estimate of the period minimum, which may have resulted from uncertainties in the neural-network analysis and photometric errors. We also provide estimated orbital periods, estimated classifications, and supplemental information on known dwarf novae with the quiescent SDSS photometry.

articleTitle: A Spectral Study of the Black Hole Candidate XTE J1752−223 in the High/Soft State with MAXI, Suzaku, and Swift
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on an X-ray spectral analysis of the black hole candidate XTE J1752<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>223 in the 2009–2010 outburst, utilizing data obtained with the MAXI/Gas Slit Camera (GSC), the Swift/XRT, and Suzaku, which work complementarily. As already reported by Nakahira et al. (2010, PASJ, 62, L27), MAXI monitored the source continuously throughout the entire outburst for about eight months. All of the MAXI/GSC energy spectra in the high/soft state, lasting for 2 months, are well represented by a multi-color disk plus power-law model. The innermost disk temperature changed from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>0.7 keV to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>0.4 keV and the disk flux decreased by an order of magnitude. Nevertheless, the innermost radius is constant at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>41 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$D_{3.5}$</tex>(cos <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$i$</tex>)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-{1}/{2}}\ $</tex>km, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$D_{3.5}$</tex> is the source distance in units of 3.5 kpc and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$i$</tex> the inclination. The multi-color disk parameters obtained with the MAXI/GSC are consistent with those with the Swift/XRT and Suzaku. The Suzaku data also suggest a possibility that the disk emission is slightly Comptonized, which could account for broad iron-K features reported previously. Assuming that the obtained innermost radius represents the innermost stable circular orbit for a non-rotating black hole, we estimate the mass of the black hole to be 5.51<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \pm\ $</tex>0.28<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ M_{\odot}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$D_{3.5}$</tex>(cos <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$i$</tex>)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-{1}/{2}}\ $</tex>, where the correction for the stress-free inner boundary condition and color hardening factor of 1.7 are taken into account. If the inclination is less than 49<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex>, as suggested from radio monitoring of transient jets, and the soft-to-hard transition in 2010 April occurred at 1%–4% of Eddignton luminosity, the fitting of the Suzaku spectra with a relativistic accretion-disk model derives constraints on the mass and the distance to be 3.1–55<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ M_{\odot}$</tex> and 2.3–22 kpc, respectively. This confirms that the compact object in XTE J1752<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>223 is a black hole.

articleTitle: Fragmentation of Primordial Filamentary Clouds under Far-Ultraviolet Radiation
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The collapse and fragmentation of uniform filamentary clouds under isotropic far-ultraviolet external radiation are investigated. Especially, the impact of the photodissociation of hydrogen molecules during collapse is considered. The dynamical and thermal evolutions of collapsing filamentary clouds are calculated by solving the virial equation and the energy equation while taking into account non-equilibrium chemical reactions. It is found that thermal evolution is hardly affected by external radiation if the initial density is high (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ n_0$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ >$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{2}$</tex> cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-3}$</tex> ). On the other hand, if the line mass of the filamentary cloud is moderate and the initial density is low (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ n_0$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \le$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{2}$</tex> cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-3}$</tex> ), the thermal evolution of the filamentary cloud tends to be adiabatic, owing to the effect of external dissociation radiation. In this case, the collapse of the filamentary cloud is suppressed, and the filamentary cloud fragments into very massive clouds (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{4-5}\ M_\odot$</tex> ) in the early stage of collapse. The analytic criterion for the filamentary clouds to fragment into such massive clouds is discussed. We also investigate the collapse and fragmentation of the filamentary clouds with an improved model. This model can partly capture the effect of run-away collapse. Also, in this model filamentary clouds with low initial density (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ n_0$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \le$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{2}$</tex> cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-3}$</tex> ) fragment into massive clouds (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{4}\ M_\odot$</tex> ) owing to the effect of external radiation.

articleTitle: A Suzaku Study of Ejecta Structure and Origin of Hard X-Ray Emission in the Supernova Remnant G 156.2+5.7
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on an X-ray study of the evolved Galactic supernova remnant (SNR) G 156.2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>5.7 based on six pointing observations with Suzaku. The remnant’s large extent (100' in diameter) allows us to investigate its radial structure in the northwestern and eastern directions from the apparent center. The X-ray spectra were well fit with a two-component non-equilibrium ionization model representing the swept-up interstellar medium (ISM) and the metal-rich ejecta. We found prominent central concentrations of Si, S, and Fe from the ejecta component; the lighter elements of O, Ne, and Mg were distributed more uniformly. The temperature of the ISM component suggests a slow shock (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>610–960 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>); hence, the remnant’s age is estimated to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>7000–15000 yr, assuming its distance to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>1.1 kpc. G 156.2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>5.7 has also been thought to emit hard, non-thermal X-rays, despite being considerably older than any other such remnant. In response to a recent discovery of a background cluster of galaxies (2XMM J045637.2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>522411), we carefully excluded its contribution, and reexamined the origin of the hard X-ray emission. We found that the residual hard X-ray emission is consistent with the expected level of the cosmic X-ray background. Thus, no robust evidence for non-thermal emission was obtained from G 156.2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>5.7. These results are consistent with the picture of an evolved SNR.

articleTitle: Slow and Fast Transitions in the Rising Phase of Outbursts from NS–LMXB Transients, Aquila X-1 and 4U 1608−52
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We analyzed the initial rising behaviors of X-ray outbursts from two transient low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) containing a neutron-star (NS), Aquila X-1 (Aql X-1) and 4U 1608<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 52, which are continuously being monitored by MAXI/GSC in 2–20 keV, RXTE/ASM in 2–10 keV, and Swift/BAT in 15–50 keV. We found that the observed ten outbursts can be classified into two types based on the patterns of the relative intensity evolutions in the two energy bands below/above 15 keV. One type behaves as the 15–50 keV intensity achieves the maximum during the initial hard-state period, and drops greatly at the hard-to-soft state transition. On the other hand, the other type does as both the 2–15 keV and 15–50 keV intensities achieve the maximums after the transition. The former have the longer initial hard-state (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ >rsim$</tex> 9 d) than the latter (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \lesssim$</tex> 5 d). Therefore, we named them as slow-type (S-type) and fast-type (F-type), respectively. These two types also show differences in the luminosity at the hard-to-soft state transition as well as in the average luminosity before the outburst started, where the S-type are higher than the F-type in both. These results suggest that the X-ray radiation during the pre-outburst period, which heats up the accretion disk and delays the disk transition (i.e., from a geometrically thick disk to a thin one), would determine whether the following outburst becomes S-type or F-type. The luminosity when the hard-to-soft state transition occurs is higher than <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 8 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{36}$</tex> erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> in the S-type, which corresponds to 4% of the Eddington luminosity for a 1.4 NS.

articleTitle: Global Structure of Optically Thin, Magnetically Supported, Two-Temperature, Black Hole Accretion Disks
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present global solutions of optically thin, two-temperature black hole accretion disks incorporating magnetic fields. We assume that the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\varpi \varphi$</tex>-component of the Maxwell stress is proportional to the total pressure, and prescribe the radial dependence of the magnetic flux advection rate in order to complete the set of basic equations. We obtained magnetically supported (low-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta $</tex>) disk solutions, whose luminosity exceeds the maximum luminosity for an advection-dominated accretion flow (ADAF), <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>rsim$</tex> 0.4<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\alpha}^2\ L_{\rm Edd}$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm Edd}$</tex> is the Eddington luminosity. The accretion flow is composed of the outer ADAF, a luminous hot accretion flow (LHAF) inside the transition layer from the outer ADAF to the low-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta $</tex> disk, the low-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta $</tex> disk, and the inner ADAF. The low-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta $</tex> disk region becomes wider as the mass-accretion rate increases further. In the low-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta $</tex> disk, the magnetic heating balances the radiative cooling, and the electron temperature decreases from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{9.5}\ $</tex>K to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{8}\ $</tex>K as the luminosity increases. These results are consistent with the anti-correlation between the energy cutoff in X-ray spectra (hence the electron temperature) and the luminosity when <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>rsim$</tex> 0.1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm Edd}$</tex>, observed in the bright/hard state during the bright hard-to-soft transitions of transient outbursts in galactic black hole candidates.

articleTitle: Radiative Transfer in Accretion Disks Under Irradiation of the Central Star
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Radiative transfer in a geometrically thin accretion disk, which is irradiated by a central star, is examined under a non-gray frequency-dependent treatment. The emergent intensity as well as other radiative quantities were analytically obtained under the Eddington approximation. In the case where the irradiation heating dominates the viscous one, the emergent spectra generally have two components. One is a multi-color blackbody part, which is reprocessed light of the irradiation flux, with a lower peak-frequency than that of the central star. The other is a single blackbody part, which is scattered light, with the same peak-frequency as that of the central star. When the vertical optical depth of the disk is small, the emergent intensity decreases in the poleward direction, but increases in the edgeward direction (limb-brightning), due to a scattering effect of the irradiated light. The overall spectra were calculated for a passive disk around a white dwarf and a neutron star. They exhibit multi-color blackbody spectra modified by the scattering light in the high-frequency region.

articleTitle: Detection of Low-Level Activities in Solar-Analog Stars from Emission Strengths of the Ca II 3934 Line
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Activity studies of solar-type stars, especially with reference to the status of our current Sun among them, have exposed the importance of (1) homogeneously selecting the sample stars and (2) reliably evaluating their activities down to a considerably low level. Motivated by these requirements, we conducted an extensive study on the activities of 118 solar-analog stars (of sufficiently similar properties to each other) by measuring the emission strength at the core of Ca II 3933.663 line (K line) on the high-dispersion spectrogram obtained by Subaru/HDS, where special attention was paid to correctly detecting the chromospheric emission by removing the wing-fitted photospheric profile calculated from the classical solar model atmosphere. This enabled us to detect low-level activities down to log r'<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 5.4 (r' is the ratio of the chromospheric core emission flux to the total bolometric flux), by which we could detect subtle activity differences that were indiscernible in previous studies. Regarding the Sun, we found log <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R'_{\odot}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 5.33 near to the low end of the distribution, which means that it belongs to the distinctly low-activity group among solar analogs. This excludes the once-suggested possibility for the high frequency of Maunder-minimum stars showing appreciably lower activities than the minimum-Sun.

articleTitle: Survey of Period Variations of Superhumps in SU UMa-Type Dwarf Novae. III. The Third Year (2010–2011)
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Continuing the project described by Kato et al. (2009, PASJ, 61, S395), we collected the times of superhump maxima for 51 SU UMa-type dwarf novae, mainly observed during the 2010–2011 season. Although most of the new data for systems with short superhump periods basically confirmed the findings by Kato et al. (ibid.) and Kato et al. (2010, PASJ, 62, 1525), the long-period system GX Cas showed an exceptionally large positive-period derivative. An analysis of public Kepler data of V344 Lyr and V1504 Cyg yielded less-striking stage transitions. In V344 Lyr, there was a prominent secondary component growing during the late stage of superoutbursts, and this component persisted for at least two more cycles of successive normal outbursts. We also investigated the superoutburst of two conspicuous eclipsing objects: HT Cas and the WZ Sge-type object SDSS J080434.20<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>510349.2. Strong beat phenomena were detected in both objects, and late-stage superhumps in the latter object had an almost constant luminosity during repeated rebrightenings. The WZ Sge-type object SDSS J133941.11<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>484727.5 showed a phase reversal around the rapid fading from the superoutburst. The object showed a prominent beat phenomenon, even after the end of the superoutburst. A pilot study of superhump amplitudes indicated that the amplitude of superhumps is strongly correlated with the orbital period, and the dependence on the inclination is weak in systems with inclinations smaller than 80<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex>.

articleTitle: Outer Rotation Curve of the Galaxy with VERA I: Trigonometric Parallax of IRAS 05168+3634
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on a measurement of the trigonometric parallax of IRAS 05168<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 3634 with VERA. The parallax is 0.532 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.053 mas, corresponding to a distance of 1.88<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{+0.21}_{-0.17}$</tex> kpc. This result is significantly smaller than the previous distance estimate of 6 kpc, based on the kinematic distance. This drastic change in the source distance revises not only the physical parameters of IRAS 05168<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 3634, but also its location of the source, placing it in the Perseus arm, rather than the Outer arm. We also measured the proper motions of the source. A combination of the distance and the proper motions with the systemic velocity yields a rotation velocity (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Theta$</tex> ) of 227<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{+\ 9}_{-11}$</tex> km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> at the source, assuming <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Theta_{\rm {0}}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 240 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> . Our result combined with previous VLBI results for six sources in the Perseus arm indicates that the sources rotate systematically slower than the Galactic rotation velocity at the LSR. In fact, we show observed disk peculiar motions averaged over the seven sources in the Perseus arm as (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ U_{\rm {mean}}$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V_{\rm {mean}}$</tex> ) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> (11 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 3, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 17 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 3) km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex>, indicating that these seven sources are systematically moving toward the Galactic center, and lag behind the Galactic rotation.

articleTitle: Suzaku Observations of Unidentified X-Ray Sources toward the Galactic Bulge
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present Suzaku observations of two unidentified sources towards the Galactic bulge, 1RXS J165256.3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>264503 and 1RXS J174459.5<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>172640, both of which were discovered with the ROSAT All-Sky Survey. We obtained wide-band spectra of these sources above 2 keV for the first time. The X-ray spectrum of 1RXS J165256.3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>264503 consists of two absorbed thin thermal plasma components with temperatures of 0.7 and 2.4 keV. An RS CVn star, HD 152178, was found within a 90% error circle of the source position. Due to this position coincidence, and an X-ray spectrum analogous to those of other RS CVn binaries, we concluded that 1RXS J165256.3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>264503 is an RS CVn-type active binary. The X-ray spectrum of 1RXS J174459.5<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>172640 was dominated by continuum emission extending up to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 20 keV, which can be explained by an absorbed cutoff power-law or a combination of absorbed multicolor disk-blackbody and Comptonized emission. We inferred that the source is a new Galactic-bulge low-mass X-ray binary (LMXB) with a luminosity of 2 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{35}$</tex> erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, based on its X-ray spectrum and lightcurve. Hence, 1RXS J174459.5<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>172640 may be an intriguing example of an LMXB in an intermediate state in which X-ray emission mechanisms can be readily explored.

articleTitle: Mode Classification of Linear Adiabatic Oscillations of Spherically Symmetric Stars
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We propose a mathematical scheme to classify the eigenmodes of linear adiabatic oscillations of spherically symmetric stars, while fully taking account of the perturbation to the gravitational potential. The scheme allows us to allocate a unique and continuous integral index (the radial order) to each non-degenerate eigenmode with a positive squared eigenfrequency of any stellar structure, whereas a pair of degenerate eigenmodes, if exist, are assigned a unique pair of indices. The indices of the eigenmodes are invariant against any continuous change in the equilibrium structure. Based on these indices, we can unambiguously define the three kinds of eigenmodes of adiabatic stellar oscillations: p-modes, g-modes, and f-modes.

articleTitle: Near-Infrared Imaging Polarization Study of M 17
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We conducted wide-field (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 8<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ '$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 8<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ '$</tex> ) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \textit{JHK}_{\rm s}$</tex> imaging polarimetric observations toward the massive star-formation region M 17. The southern H II bar is identified as large-scale infrared reflection nebula (IRN) illuminated by OB stars in the cluster center, while the northern bar shows polarization originating from dichroic extinction. Three small-scale bipolar IRN with centro-symmetric polarization patterns were identified, and their illuminating sources, embedded young stellar objects (YSOs), are most likely the driving sources of bipolar outflows. <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \textit{JHK}_{\rm s}$</tex> polarizations of point sources in M 17 show a wavelength dependence of the polarization of dichroic extinction in the general interstellar medium, indicating <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 1.8 for the empirical relation <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ P$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \propto$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \lambda^{-\alpha}$</tex> of interstellar polarization. The distribution of the polarization angle shows two peaks at 170<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{\circ}$</tex> and 110<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{\circ}$</tex>, indicating a non-uniform magnetic field structure in M 17. The direction of the magnetic field in the cluster region is south-north. However, the magnetic field in the H II region is roughly between 100<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{\circ}$</tex> –140<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{\circ}$</tex>, roughly perpendicular to the Galactic disk. Such a configuration indicates that the magnetic field in the cluster region is twisted from the primordial orientation in the cluster formation. The magnetic field in the southern bar has a total strength of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 230<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \ \mu$</tex> G, and is 40<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{\circ}$</tex> inclined to the plane of the sky. The outflows driven by YSOs in M 17 show a poor relation with the surrounding magnetic fields. This fact implies that the magnetic field in M 17 does not dominate the orientations of protostars formed inside.

articleTitle: Search for Diffuse X-Rays from the Bow Shock Region of Runaway Star BD +43 3654 with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The bow shocks of runaway stars with strong stellar winds of over 2000 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> can serve as particle acceleration sites. The conversion from stellar wind luminosity into particle acceleration power has an efficiency of the same order of magnitude as those in supernova remnants, based on the radio emission from the bow shock region of runaway star BD <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 43 3654 (Benaglia et al. 2010, A&A, 517, L10). If this object exhibits typical characteristics, then runaway star systems can contribute a non-negligible fraction of Galactic cosmic-ray electrons. To constrain the maximum energy of accelerated particles from measurements of possible non-thermal emissions in the X-ray band, Suzaku observed BD <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 43 3654 in 2011 April with an exposure of 99 ks. Because the onboard instruments have a stable and low background level, Suzaku detected a possible enhancement over the background of 7.6 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 3.4 counts arcmin<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-2}$</tex> at the bow shock region, where the error represents the 3 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sigma$</tex> statistics only. However, the excess is not significant within the systematic errors of non-X-ray and cosmic-ray backgrounds of the X-ray Imaging Spectrometer, which are <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 6.0 and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 34 counts arcmin<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-2}$</tex>, respectively, and the 3 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sigma$</tex> upper limit in the X-ray luminosity from the shock region, which is 1.1 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{32}$</tex> erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> per 41.2 arcmin<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^2$</tex> in the 0.5 to 10 keV band. This result leads to three conclusions: (1) a shock-heating process is inefficient on this system; (2) the maximum energy of electrons does not exceed <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 10 TeV, corresponding to a Lorentz factor of less than <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ 10^7$</tex> ; and (3) the magnetic field in the shock acceleration site might not be as turbulent as those in pulsar wind nebulae and supernova remnants.

articleTitle: Conditions of Gravitational Instability in Protoplanetary Disks
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Gravitational instability is one of the considerable mechanisms to explain the formation of giant planets. We have studied the gravitational stability in protoplanetary disks around a protostar. The temperature and Toomre's <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ Q$</tex> value were calculated by assuming local equilibrium between viscous heating and radiative cooling (local thermal equilibrium). We assumed a constant <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha$</tex> viscosity and used a cooling function with realistic opacity. Then, we derived the critical surface density, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Sigma_{\rm {c}}$</tex>, that is needed in order for a disk to become gravitationally unstable as a function of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ r$</tex> . This critical surface density, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Sigma _{\rm c}$</tex>, is strongly affected by the temperature dependence of the opacity. At a radius of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ r_{\rm c}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 20 AU, where ices form, the value of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Sigma _{\rm c}$</tex> changes discontinuously by one order of magnitude. This <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Sigma _{\rm c}$</tex> is determined only by a local thermal process and the criterion of gravitational instability. By comparing a given surface density profile with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Sigma _{\rm c}$</tex>, one can discuss the gravitational instability of protoplanetary disks. As an example, we discuss the gravitational instability of two semianalytic models for protoplanetary disks. One is a steady state accretion disk, which is realized after viscous evolution. The other is a disk that has the same angular-momentum distribution as its parent cloud core, which corresponds to the disk that has just formed. As a result, it is found that the disk tends to become gravitationally unstable for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ r$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \ge$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ r_{\rm c}$</tex> because ices make the disk temperature low. In a region closer to the protostar than <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ r_{\rm c}$</tex>, it is difficult for a typical protoplanetary disk to fragment because of the high temperature and the large Coriolis force. Based on this result, we conclude that fragmentation near the central star is possible, but difficult.

articleTitle: Fundamental Parameters of the Milky Way Galaxy Based on VLBI Astrometry
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present analyses to determine the fundamental parameters of the Galaxy based on VLBI astrometry of 52 Galactic maser sources obtained with VERA, VLBA, and EVN. We model the Galaxy's structure with a set of parameters, including the Galaxy center distance <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ R_0$</tex>, the angular rotation velocity at the LSR <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Omega_0$</tex>, the mean peculiar motion of the sources with respect to Galactic rotation (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ U_{\rm src}$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V_{\rm src}$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ W_{\rm src}$</tex> ), the rotation-curve shape index, and the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V$</tex> component of the Solar peculiar motions, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V_\odot $</tex> . Based on a Markov chain Monte-Carlo method, we find that the Galaxy center distance is constrained at a 5% level to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ R_0$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 8.05 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.45 kpc, where the error bar includes both statistical and systematic errors. We also find that the two components of the source peculiar motion <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ U_{\rm src}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ W_{\rm src}$</tex> are fairly small compared to the Galactic rotation velocity, being <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ U_{\rm src}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 1.0 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 1.5 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ W_{\rm src}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 1.4 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 1.2 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> . Also, the rotation curve shape is found to be basically flat between Galacto-centric radii of 4 and 13 kpc. On the other hand, we find a linear relation between <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V_{\rm src}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V_\odot $</tex> as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V_{\rm src}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V_\odot $</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 19 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 2) km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex>, suggesting that the value of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V_{\rm src}$</tex> is fully dependent on the adopted value of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V_\odot $</tex> . Regarding the rotation speed in the vicinity of the Sun, we also find a strong correlation between <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Omega_0$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V_\odot $</tex> . We find that the angular velocity of the Sun, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Omega_{\odot}$</tex>, which is defined as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Omega_\odot$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \equiv$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Omega_0$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V_\odot/R_0$</tex>, can be well constrained with the best estimate of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Omega_\odot$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 31.09 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.78 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> kpc<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> . This corresponds to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Theta_0$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 238 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 14 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> if one adopts the above value of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ R_0$</tex> and recent determination of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V_\odot $</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 12 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex>.

articleTitle: A Variable Partial Covering Model for the Seyfert 1 Galaxy MCG −6–30–15
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We propose a simple spectral model for the Seyfert 1 Galaxy MCG <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 6–30–15 that can explain most of the 1–40 keV spectral variation by a change of the partial covering fraction, similar to that proposed by Miller, Turner, and Reeves (2008, A&A, 483, 437). Our spectral model is composed of three continuum components: (1) a direct power-law component, (2) a heavily absorbed power-law component by mildly ionized intervening matter, and (3) a cold-disk reflection component far from the black hole with a moderate solid-angle (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Omega/$</tex> 2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pi$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \simeq$</tex> 0.3) accompanying a narrow fluorescent iron line. The first two components are affected by the surrounding thin highly ionized absorber with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ N_{\rm H}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \simeq$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{23.4}$</tex> cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-2}$</tex> and log <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \xi$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \simeq$</tex> 3.4. The heavy absorber in the second component is fragmented into many clouds, each of which is composed of radial zones with different ionization states and different column densities, a main body (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ N_{\rm H}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \simeq$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{24.2}$</tex> cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-2}$</tex>, log <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \xi$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \simeq$</tex> 1.6), an envelope (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ N_{\rm H}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \simeq$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{22.1}$</tex> cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-2}$</tex>, log <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \xi$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \simeq$</tex> 1.9), and presumably a completely opaque core. Not only the intrinsic spectral shape of the X-ray source but also these parameters of the ionized absorbers are unchanged at all. The central X-ray source extends moderately, and its luminosity is not significantly variable. The observed flux and spectral variations are mostly explained by the variation of the geometrical partial covering fraction of the central source ranging from 0 (uncovered) to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim\ $</tex> 0.63 by the intervening ionized clouds in the line of sight. The ionized iron K-edge of the heavily absorbed component explains most of the seemingly broad line-like features, a well-known spectral characteristic of MCG <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 6–30–15. The direct component and the absorbed one are negatively correlated, and their variations cancel out each other, so that the fractional spectral variation becomes the minimum at the iron-energy band; thus, another observational characteristic of MCG <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 6–30–15 is explained.

articleTitle: Star Formation and AGN Activity in Galaxies Classified Using the 1.6 μm Bump and PAH Features at z = 0.4–2
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We studied the star-formation and AGN activity of massive galaxies in the redshift range <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0.4–2, which were detected in a deep survey field using the AKARI InfraRed (IR) astronomical satellite and Subaru telescope toward the North Ecliptic Pole (NEP). The AKARI/IRC Mid-InfraRed (MIR) multiband photometry was used to trace the star-forming activities with Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon (PAH) emission, which is effective not only to distinguish between star-forming and AGN galaxies, but also to estimate the Star Formation Rate (SFR) with converting its flux to the total emitting IR (TIR) luminosity. In combination with the analyses of the stellar components, we studied the MIR SED features of star-forming and AGN-harboring galaxies, which we summarize below: (1) The rest-frame 7.7-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \mu $</tex> m and 5-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \mu $</tex> m luminosities are good tracers of star-forming and AGN activities from their PAH and dusty tori emissions, respectively. (2) For dusty star-forming galaxies without AGN, their SFR shows a correlation that is nearly proportional to their stellar mass, and their specific SFR (sSFR) per unit stellar mass increases with redshift. Extinctions estimated from their TIR luminosities are larger than those from their optical SED fittings, which may be caused by geometric variations of dust in them. (3) Even for dusty star-forming galaxies with AGN, SFRs can be derived from their TIR luminosities with subtraction of the obscured AGN contribution, which indicates that their SFRs were possibly quenched around <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \simeq$</tex> 0.8 compared with those without AGN. (4) The AGN activity from their rest-frame 5-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \mu $</tex> m luminosity suggests that their Super Massive Black Holes (SMBHs) could already have grown to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \simeq$</tex> 3 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{8}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ M_{\odot}$</tex> in most massive galaxies with 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{11}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ M_{\odot}$</tex> at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ <$</tex> 1.2, and the mass relation between SMBHs and their host galaxies has already become established by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \simeq$</tex> 1–2.

articleTitle: Formation of Dense Gas and Stars near the End of the Galactic Bar
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We carried out H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{13}$</tex> CO<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{+}$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ J$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 1–0) observations of a molecular cloud containing a massive star-forming region, G23.44<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 0.18, using the Nobeyama 45-m radio telescope. We identified three clumps, named Clumps A, B, and C, on the periphery of the H II region in the cloud. The most massive clump, Clump A, has a radius of 0.74 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.20 pc and a mass of 1100<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{+800}_{-\hskip.35mm 640}\ M\odot$</tex> . Both Clumps B and C, however, have much smaller size and mass than Clump A. These three clumps seem not to be virialized. We also found four sub-clumps in Clump A. These sub-clumps may be affected by the strong outflow penetrating Clump A. The star-formation efficiency (SFE) of the entire cloud is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 0.4%, which is typical for galactic star-forming clouds. The SFE of Clump A is 25<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{+14}_{-\hskip.35mm 11}$</tex> %. This value is higher than other embedded cluster-forming clumps, which implies that stars, including massive ones, are formed efficiently and actively in Clump A. The dense gas fraction estimated from H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{13}$</tex> CO<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{+}$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ J$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 1–0) and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{13}$</tex> CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ J$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 1–0) of the cloud are lower than those of other star-forming regions. The results mean that this star-forming region is young, and suggest that the formation of dense gas and stars in the cloud has just begun. Comparing the dynamical age of the H II region with the fragmentation timescale for the collect and collapse process, molecular gas is accumulating through expansion of the H II region in Clumps B and C. Since there are massive young stellar objects (YSOs) in Clump A, we suggest that this clump has already become denser than the other regions in the cloud due to converging flow, or some external factors, such as an old bubble and cloud–cloud interaction.

articleTitle: Optimization by Smoothed Bandpass Calibration in Radio Spectroscopy
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have developed the Smoothed Bandpass Calibration (SBC) method and the best suitable scan pattern to optimize radio spectroscopic observations. Adequate spectral smoothing is applied to the spectrum toward OFF-source blank sky adjacent to a target source for the purpose of bandpass correction. Because the smoothing process reduces noise, we can reduce the integration time for OFF-source scans while keeping the signal-to-noise ratio. Since smoothing is not applied to ON-source scans, the spectral resolution for line features is maintained. An optimal smoothing window is determined by the bandpass flatness evaluated by the spectral Allan variance (SAV). An efficient scan pattern is designed for OFF-source scans within the bandpass-stability time scale estimated by the time-based Allan variance (TAV). We tested the SBC using a digital spectrometer, VESPA, at the VERA Iriki station. For a targeted noise level of 5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex>10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-4}$</tex> as its ratio to the system noise, the optimal smoothing window was 32–60 channels (ch) over the whole bandwidth of 1024 ch, and the optimal scan pattern was designed as a sequence of 70 s ON <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 10 s OFF scan pairs. The noise level by the SBC has been improved by a factor of 1.74, compared with that by the conventional method. The total telescope-time to reach our target with the SBC was 400 s, which is 1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ /$</tex> 3 of 1200 s required in the conventional way. Improvements in the telescope-time efficiency with the SBC were calculated to be 3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> (for single-beam scans), 2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> (dual-beam), and 1.3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> (on-the-fly). The SBC is useful for optimizing scan patterns for observations from now on, and also for improving the signal-to-noise ratios of archival data if ON- and OFF-source spectra are separately recorded, though the efficiency depends on the spectral stability of the receiving system.

articleTitle: Annual Parallax of the K-Type Star System IRAS 22480+6002 Measured with VERA
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present astrometric VLBI observations of H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex> O masers associated with IRAS 22480<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex> 6002 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> IRC<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex> 60370, hereafter I22480) with the VLBI Exploration of Radio Astrometry (VERA). The stellar type of I22480 looks unusual in stellar maser sources, and has been debated since the 1970's. We successfully determined that an annual parallax of a group of H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex> O maser spots is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pi$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 0.400 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex> 0.025 mas, corresponding to a distance to I22480 of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$D$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 2.50<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+0.17}_{-0.15}$</tex> kpc. This suggests that an estimated bolometric luminosity of I22480 should be revised to 35000 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\odot}$</tex>, preferring a K-type supergiant to an RV Tau-type variable star, previously suggested. Although its spectral type is unusual in stellar maser sources, internal motions of H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex> O maser features suggest that the H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex> O masers are associated with the circumstellar envelope of this star. We derived a secular proper motion of I22480, (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu_{\alpha}$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu_{\delta}$</tex> ) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 2.58 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex> 0.33, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 1.91 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex> 0.17) [mas yr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> ], from a possible stellar motion relative to the maser feature motion. The derived motion of I22480 in the Milky Way has a deviation of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim-$</tex> 30 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> in the Galactic azimuthal direction from the circular motion, estimated from a galactocentric distance to I22480 and an assumption of a flat Galactic rotation curve. This peculiar motion is still comparable to those typically seen in H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex> O maser sources located in the Perseus Arm. Taking into account its peculiar motion and proximity to the Galactic midplane (z<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\simeq$</tex> 60 pc), I22480 may be a member of the Galactic thin disk.

articleTitle: Accretion Geometry of the Low-Mass X-Ray Binary Aquila X-1 in the Soft and Hard States
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The neutron-star Low-Mass X-ray Binary Aquila X-1 was observed seven times in total with the Suzaku X-ray observatory from September 28 to October 30 in 2007, in the decaying phase of an outburst. In order to constrain the flux-dependent accretion geometry of this source over wider energy bands than employed in most previous studies, the present study utilized two out of seven data sets. The 0.8–31 keV spectrum on September 28, taken with the XIS and HXD-PIN for an exposure of 13.8 ks, shows an absorbed 0.8–31 keV flux of 3.6 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-9}$</tex> erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex>, together with typical characteristics of the soft state of this type of object. The spectrum was successfully explained by an optically thick disk emission plus a Comptonized blackbody component. Although these results are in general agreement with previous studies, the significance of a hard tail recently reported using the same data was inconclusive in our analysis. The spectrum acquired on October 9 for an exposure of 19.7 ks was detected over a 0.8–100 keV band with the XIS, HXD-PIN, and HXD-GSO, at an absorbed flux of 8.5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-10}$</tex> erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex> (in 0.8–100 keV). It shows characteristics of the hard state, and was successfully explained by the same two continuum components, but with rather different parameters, including much stronger thermal Comptonization, of which the seed photon source was identified with blackbody emission from the neutron-star surface. As a result, the accretion flow in the hard state is inferred to take the form of an optically-thick and geometrically-thin disk down to a radius of 21 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex> 4 km from the neutron star, and then turn into an optically thin nearly spherical hot flow.

articleTitle: X-Ray Groups of Galaxies at 0.5 1 in zCOSMOS: Increased AGN Activities in High Redshift Groups
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present a photometric and spectroscopic study of galaxies at 0.5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$<$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${z}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$<$</tex> 1 as a function of the environment based on data from the zCOSMOS survey. There is a fair amount of evidence that galaxy properties depend on the mass of groups and clusters, in the sense that quiescent galaxies prefer more massive systems. We base our analysis on a mass-selected environment using X-ray groups of galaxies, and define the group membership using a large number of spectroscopic redshifts from zCOSMOS. We show that the fraction of red galaxies is higher in groups than in the field at all redshifts probed in our study. Interestingly, the fraction of [O II] emitters on the red sequence increases at higher redshifts in groups, while the fraction does not strongly evolve in the field. This is due to increased dusty star-formation activities and/or increased activities of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) in high-redshift groups. We investigate these possibilities using the 30-band photometry and X-ray data. We find that the stellar population of the red [O II] emitters in groups is old, and there is no clear hint of dusty star-formation activities in those galaxies. The observed increase of red [O II] emitters in groups is likely due to increased AGN activities. However, since our overall statistics are poor, any firm conclusions need to be drawn from a larger statistical sample of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${z}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 1 groups.

articleTitle: Standing Kink Waves with Longitudinal Flow in Fine Threaded Coronal Loops: A New Method for the Coronal Seismology through Beat and Damped Waves
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Stimulated by the first weakly attenuated standing kink oscillations of coronal fine threads filled with cool flowing plasma, seen in a recent Ca II H-line observed by Solar Optical Telescope (SOT) aboard Hinode, in this study we present the effects of longitudinal flow on the standing wave. We have found that flow generates two important consequences: first, it produces a frequency shift, which leads to the phenomenon of wave beating; second, it splits the damping time of the forward and backward waves of the attenuated standing wave (considered here only the resonance absorption) into two different values. A comparative analysis of the beat waves, within the “quarter-beat period approximation” together with attenuated waves, seems to be very appealing for coronal seisomology. We refer a new parameter, modulating time (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\tau_{\rm m}$</tex>), which is defined as the time when the amplitude of the beat wave becomes zero for a wave train that lies within a quarter period of the beat envelope, the so-called “quarter beat period approximation”. We can compare this <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\tau_{\rm m}$</tex> with the attenuating time (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\tau_{\rm D}$</tex>) to discriminate the behaviour of the signal, as follows: if <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\tau_{\rm m}~>~\tau_{\rm D}$</tex>, the envelope of the signal is dominated by attenuation due to resonance absorption, while if <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\tau_{\rm m}~<~\tau_{\rm D}$</tex>, the envelope of the signal is dominated by modulation due to beating. Since observation corresponds to first inequality, the amplitude of the signal seems to be dominated by attenuation due to resonance absorption. Hence, the inequality <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\tau_{\rm m}~\geq~\tau_{\rm D}$</tex> imposes an upper bounds for the density contrast and magnetic field for a given value of the observed flow. Besides these, we also find that the flow-generated splitting of the damping time also leads to an <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>8%–10% uncertainty in our estimation of the radial inhomogeneity across the loop boundary, as compared to the static case, i.e., when the flow is zero.

articleTitle: Trapped, Two-Armed, Nearly Vertical Oscillations in Disks with Toroidal Magnetic Fields II: Effects of Finite Thickness
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We examine the radial trapping of two-armed (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ m$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 2) vertical p-mode oscillations in geometrically thin relativistic disks that are vertically isothermal, but terminated at a certain height by the presence of hot and low-density corona. The disks are assumed to be subject to toroidal magnetic fields. The oscillations are classified by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ n$</tex>, a number related to the node number of oscillations in the vertical direction, and starting from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ n$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 1. In modes with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ n$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 1, the frequencies of trapped oscillations depend little on the height of termination, but in modes with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ n$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 2, 3, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \cdots$</tex> the frequencies decrease and the radial extentions of the trapped region become wide, as the termination height decreases. This study is a preparation to examine whether these oscillations can describe kilo-hertz quasi-periodic oscillations (kHz QPOs), horizontal branch oscillations (HBOs), and their correlations.

articleTitle: 13CO(J = 1–0) On-the-Fly Mapping of the Giant H II Region NGC 604: Variation in Molecular Gas Density and Temperature due to Sequential Star Formation
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 1–0) line emission observations with the Nobeyama 45-m telescope toward the giant H II region NGC 604 in the spiral galaxy M 33. We detected <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 1–0) line emissions in 3 major giant molecular clouds (GMCs) labeled as GMC-A, B, and C beginning at the north. We derived two line intensity ratios, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 1–0)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$/$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 1–0), <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{13/12}$</tex>, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 3–2)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$/$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 1–0), <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{31}$</tex>, for each GMC at an angular resolution of 25” (100 pc). The averaged values of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{13/12}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{31}$</tex> are 0.06 and 0.31 within the whole GMC-A, 0.11 and 0.67 within the whole GMC-B, and 0.05 and 0.36 within the whole GMC-C, respectively. In addition, we obtained <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{13/12}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 0.09<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \pm\ $</tex>0.02 and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{31}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 0.76<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \pm\ $</tex>0.06 at the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 1–0) peak position of the GMC-B.
