Under the Large Velocity Gradient approximation, we determined a gas density of 2.8 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{3}\ $</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex> and a kinetic temperature of 33<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+9}_{-5}\ $</tex>K at the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 1–0) peak position of the GMC-B. Moreover, we determined 2.5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{3}\ $</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex> and 25<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \pm\ $</tex>2 K as the averaged values within the whole GMC-B. We concluded that dense molecular gas is formed everywhere in the GMC-B because the derived gas density not only at the peak position of the GMC, but also averaged over the whole GMC, exceeds 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{3}\ $</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex>. On the other hand, the kinetic temperature averaged over the whole GMC-B, 25 K, is significantly lower than that at the peak position, 33 K. This is because the H II regions are lopsided to the northern part of the GMC-B; thus, OB stars can heat only the northern part, including the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 1–0) peak position, of this GMC.

articleTitle: Reconstruction of the Structure of Accretion Disks in Dwarf Novae from the Multi-Band Light Curves of Early Superhumps
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We propose a new method to reconstruct the structure of accretion disks in dwarf novae using multi-band light curves of early superhumps. Our model assumes that early superhumps are caused by the rotation effect of non-axisymmetrically flaring disks. We have developed a Bayesian model for this reconstruction, in which a smoother disk-structure tends to have a higher prior probability. We analyzed simultaneous optical and near-infrared photometric data of early superhumps of the dwarf nova, V455 And using this technique. The reconstructed disk has two flaring parts in the outermost region of the disk. These parts are responsible for the primary and secondary maxima of the light curves. The height-to-radius ratio is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ h/r$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0.20–0.25 in the outermost region. In addition to the outermost flaring structures, flaring arm-like patterns can be seen in an inner region of the reconstructed disk. The overall profile of the reconstructed disk is reminiscent of the disk structure that is deformed by the tidal effect. However, an inner arm-like pattern, which is responsible for the secondary minimum in the light curve, cannot be reproduced only by the tidal effect. It implies the presence of another mechanism that deforms the disk structure. Alternatively, the temperature distribution of the disk could be non-axisymmetric. We demonstrate that the disk structure with weaker arm-like patterns is optimal in the model including the irradiation effect. However, the strongly irradiated disk gives quite blue colors, which may conflict with the observation. Our results suggest that the amplitude of early superhumps depends mainly on the height of the outermost flaring regions of the disk. We predict that early superhumps can be detected with an amplitude of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ >$</tex> 0.02 mag in about 90% of WZ Sge stars.

articleTitle: Estimates of Emission-Region Locations of Fermi Flat-Spectrum Radio Quasars
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have studied the location of emission regions through modeling the quasi-simultaneous multifrequency spectral energy distributions of 21 Fermi flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs) in the frame of a multicomponent one-zone leptonic model. In our calculations, we took the detailed broad line region (BLR) structure into account, and discussed the effect of the uncertainty of the BLR structure on constraining the location of the emission regions for each FSRQ; besides, we also included both the internal and the external absorptions. Our results indicate that: (1) the contribution of the external Compton-BLR component to the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \gamma$</tex>-ray emission is important, and the energy density of external target-photon fields depends on the location of the emission region, which can be derived by reproducing the observed <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \gamma$</tex>-ray emission; (2) the emission regions of FSRQs with relatively low accretion-disk luminosity lie in the region of (7.9 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{16}$</tex> –1.3 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{18})$</tex> cm (300–4300 Schwarzschild radii) from central black hole, and for FSRQs with high accretion-disk luminosity, the emission regions are located in a larger region of (2.6 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{17}$</tex> –4.2 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{18}$</tex> ) cm (300–5600 Schwarzschild radii).

articleTitle: A Study on the Orbital Period Variation of AR Lacertae
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In this paper, we collect all available times of the light minimum of AR Lac from the literature and databases. Through an analysis of the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ O$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ C$</tex> curve by a weighted least-squares method, we found that the orbital period of the system shows a cyclic oscillation with a period of 50.93 yr superimposed on a long-term secular period decrease at a rate of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ dP/dt$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> (2.128 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.060) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-9}$</tex> d<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ /$</tex> d. Since both components of AR Lac are late-type stars, and show strong Ca H and K emission lines, the orbital period variation may be caused by the magnetic activity of the system.

articleTitle: Spectral Evolutions in Gamma-Ray Burst Exponential Decays Observed with Suzaku WAM
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: This paper presents a study on the spectral evolution of gamma-ray burst (GRB) prompt emissions observed with the Suzaku Wide-band All-sky Monitor (WAM). By making use of the WAM data archive, 6 bright GRBs exhibiting 7 well-separated fast-rise-exponential-decay (FRED) shaped light curves are presented, and the evaluated exponential decay time constants of the energy-resolved light curves from these FRED peak light curves are shown to indicate significant spectral evolution. The energy dependence of the time constants is well described with a power-law function, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\tau$</tex>(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E$</tex>) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\propto$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E^\gamma$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>(0.34<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm $</tex>0.12) on average, although 5 FRED peaks show a consistent value of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$/$</tex>2, which is expected in synchrotron or inverse-Compton cooling models. In particular, 2 of the GRBs were located with accuracy sufficient to evaluate the time-resolved spectra with precise energy response matrices. Their behavior in spectral evolution suggests two different origins of emissions. In the case of GRB 081224, the derived 1-s time-resolved spectra are well described by a blackbody radiation model with a power-law component. The derived behavior of cooling is consistent with that expected from radiative cooling or expansion of the emission region. On the other hand, the other 1-s time-resolved spectra from GRB 100707A is well described by a Band GRB model as well as with the thermal model. Although relative poor statistics prevent us to conclude, the energy dependence in the decaying light curve is consistent with that expected in the former emission mechanism model.

articleTitle: NH$_{3}$ Survey Observation of Massive Star-Forming Region W 43
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We consider the properties of giant molecular cloud complexes in the star-forming region W 43 with a resolution of several pc scale, and discuss their relations to the evolutionary stages of massive star formation. We performed a NH<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{3}$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K$</tex>) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> (1, 1), (2, 2), and (3, 3) inversion-line survey with the Hokkaido University 11-m telescope. Among 51 observed positions, selected based on integrated intensity maps of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 1–0), these three emissions were detected from 21, 8, and 5 positions, respectively. The integrated intensity of the NH<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{3}$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K$</tex>) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> (1, 1) line was found to be proportional to the far-infrared luminosity, estimated from IRAS data. The rotation temperatures were deduced to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>15–20 K at eight observed positions. In addition, the upper limits were estimated for 13 positions, which include the relatively low temperatures below 14 K at two positions with a relatively high fractions of NH<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{3}$</tex> for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO and with a low far-infrared luminosity. We derived the ortho-to-para abundance ratio of NH<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{3}$</tex>. From the population distribution between the ortho- and para-levels of NH<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{3}$</tex>, we also derived temperatures of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>6–12 K, which may be interpreted as the temperatures when NH<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{3}$</tex> molecules were formed. We discuss the relevance of the present results of our observations to the massive star-formation process and the current status of the W 43 region while taking into account previous observations of other indicators of massive star formation. It is shown that the complexes contain several regions in different evolutionary stages, or with the distinct characteristics of star formation within a timescales shorter than the lifetime of massive stars.

articleTitle: Peculiar Black-Hole Unipolar Induction
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: It is argued that a posteriori without conflicting with the dubbed no-hair theorem, a Kerr black hole acquires its own proper magnetosphere in the steady eigen-state. The angular frequency of field lines, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ {\Omega_{\rm F}}$</tex>, given as the eigenvalue in terms of the hole’s angular frequency, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ {\Omega_{\rm H}}$</tex>, couples with the frame-dragging angular frequency, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \omega$</tex>, to create an inner general-relativistic domain of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ {\Omega_{\rm H}} > \omega$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ > {\Omega_{\rm F}}$</tex>, in which the gradient of the electric potential is, when viewed by the fiducial observers (FIDOs), reversed in direction from that in the outer quasi-classical domain of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ {\Omega_{\rm F}} > \omega$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ >$</tex> 0. The field lines are pinned down in the plasma source at the interface between the two domains (upper null surface S<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ _{\rm N}$</tex> ), from which pair-particles well up, charge-separated into the ingoing and outgoing winds. The EMFs due to unipolar induction operate to drive the surface currents, following Ohm’s law, on the resistive membranes terminating the force-free domains (say, S<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ _{\rm ffH}$</tex> and S<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ _{{\rm ff}\infty}$</tex> ), to exert the surface torques onto the respective membranes, thereby extracting angular momentum from the hole and transferring to the domain of astrophysical loads.

articleTitle: Magnetic Helicity of Solar Active Regions as Revealed by Vector Magnetograms and Coronal X-Ray Images
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have used photospheric vector magnetograms of 15 different solar active regions to calculate the current helicity parameter, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha _{\rm av}$</tex>, and the linear force-free field (LFFF) parameter, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha _{\rm best}$</tex>, that fits best the observed transverse field. The data were obtained with the Solar Magnetic Field Telescope at the Huairou Solar Observing Station, the National Astronomical Observatories of China, the Solar Flare Telescope of the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan, and the Haleakala Stokes Polarimeter at the Mees Solar Observatory, University of Hawaii, from 1997 to 2000. The agreement in sign of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha _{\rm av}$</tex> between three vector magnetographs is better than 90%. For <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha _{\rm best}$</tex>, the agreement is 80%–90%. The line-of-sight magnetograms observed with the Michelson–Doppler Imager (MDI) on SOHO and coronal X-ray images observed with the Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT) on Yohkoh have been used to determine the constant <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha _{\rm c}$</tex> of the LFFF in the corona. The value of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha _{\rm c}$</tex> corresponds to the extrapolated coronal field whose field lines best match, by visual inspection, the structure of coronal loops in X-ray images. It is found that the sign agreement between photospheric <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha _{\rm av}$</tex> or <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha _{\rm best}$</tex> and coronal <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha _{\rm c}$</tex> is lower (60%–85%). We consider the differences in measurements, observing conditions, data reduction methods, and limitation in LFFF extrapolation, and discuss their contributions to the dispersions in the hemispheric sign rule of helicity.

articleTitle: Destructible Bars in Disk Galaxies under the Dynamical Influence of a Massive Central Black Hole
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The characteristics of the galactic bars that are prone to suffer a damaging impact from a massive central black hole are examined using flat stellar disks. We construct three disk model groups that consist of exponential disks with one type of velocity distribution and Kuzmin–Toomre disks with two different types of exact equilibrium distribution functions. For each disk model group, three disks that have different typical Toomre’s <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$Q$</tex> values are evolved to form bars through dynamical instability. Once a bar is fully developed, a black hole (BH), whose mass is 1% of the disk mass, is adiabatically added at the center of the disk. Our results show that lower-amplitude bars, that is weaker bars, are dissolved more easily by that BH. We have found that this destructibility is rooted in the characteristic feature that the bar formed spontaneously becomes shorter in length and rounder in shape with decreasing bar amplitude. Since such weaker bars are found to originate from colder disks in each disk model group, it follows that for a given form of velocity structure, the coldness of an initial disk determines whether the bar produced in that disk is favorable to dissolution induced by a massive central BH. In addition, the existence of bar-dissolved galaxies of the kind studied here is also discussed.

articleTitle: Extremely Strong 13CO J = 3→2 Line in the ``Water Fountain'' IRAS 16342−3814: Evidence for the Hot-Bottom Burning
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We observed four ``water fountain'' sources in the CO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ J$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \rightarrow$</tex> 2 line emission with the Atacama Submillimeter Telescope Experiment (ASTE) 10 m telescope in 2010–2011. The water fountain sources are evolved stars that form high-velocity collimated jets traced by H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ _{2}$</tex> O maser emission. The CO line was detected only from IRAS 16342<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 3814. The present work confirmed that the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{12}$</tex> CO to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{13}$</tex> CO line intensity ratio is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 1.5 at the systemic velocity. We discuss the origins of the very low <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{12}$</tex> CO-to-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{13}$</tex> CO intensity ratio, as possible evidence for ``hot-bottom burning'' in an oxygen-rich star, and the CO intensity variation in IRAS 16342<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 3814.

articleTitle: Statistical Analyses of White-Light Flares: Two Main Results about Flare Behaviour
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present two main results, based on models and the statistical analyses of 1672 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ U$</tex>-band flares. We also discuss the behaviour of white-light flares. In addition, the parameters of the flares detected from two years of observations on CR Dra are presented. By comparing with flare parameters obtained from other UV Ceti-type stars, we examine the behaviour of the optical flare processes along with the spectral types. Moreover, we aimed, using large white-light flare data, to analyse the flare time-scales with respect to some results obtained from X-ray observations. Using SPSS V17.0 and GraphPad Prism V5.02 software, the flares detected from CR Dra were modelled with the OPEA function, and analysed with the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ t$</tex>-Test method to compare similar flare events in other stars. In addition, using some regression calculations in order to derive the best histograms, the time-scales of white-light flares were analysed. Firstly, CR Dra flares have revealed that white-light flares behave in a similar way as their counterparts observed in X-rays. As can be seen in X-ray observations, the electron density seems to be a dominant parameter in white-light flare process, too. Secondly, the distributions of the flare time-scales demonstrate that the number of observed flares reaches a maximum value in some particular ratios, which are 0.5, or its multiples, and especially positive integers. The thermal processes might be dominant for these white-light flares, while non-thermal processes might be dominant in the others. To obtain better results for the behaviour of the white-light flare process along with the spectral types, much more stars in a wide spectral range, from spectral type dK5e to dM6e, must be observed in white-light flare patrols.

articleTitle: Combined Spectral and Timing Analysis of the Black Hole Candidate MAXI J1659−152, Discovered by MAXI and Swift
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on X-ray spectral and timing results of a new black hole candidate (BHC), MAXI J1659<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>152, with an orbital period of 2.41 hr (shortest among BHCs) in a 2010 outburst from 65 Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) observations and 8 simultaneous Swift and RXTE observations. According to the definitions of the spectral states in Remillard and McClintock (2006, ARA&A, 44, 49), most of the observations have been classified into the intermediate state. All of the X-ray broadband spectra can be modeled by a multi-color disk plus a power-law with an exponential cutoff or a multi-color disk plus a Comptonization component. During the initial phase of the outburst, a high-energy cutoff was visible at 30–40 keV. The innermost radius of the disk gradually decreased by a factor of more than 3 from the onset of the outburst, and reached a constant value of 35<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ d_{10}$</tex>cos<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ i$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1/2}$</tex> km, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ d_{10}$</tex> is the distance in units of 10 kpc and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ i$</tex> is the inclination. The type-C quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) frequency varied from 1.6 Hz to 7.3 Hz in association with a change of the innermost radius, while the innermost radius remained constant during the type-B QPO detections at 1.6–4.1 Hz. Hence, we suggest that the origin of the type-B QPOs is different from that of type-C QPOs, the latter of which would originate from the disk truncation radius. Assuming the constant innermost radius in the latter phase of the outburst as the innermost stable circular orbit, the black hole mass in MAXI J1659<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>152 is estimated to be 3.6–8.0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ M_{\odot}$</tex> for a distance of 5.3–8.6 kpc and an inclination angle of 60<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex>–75<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex>.

articleTitle: Relativistic Radiative Transfer in Relativistic Plane–Parallel Flows: Roles of Scattering Effect
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Relativistic radiative transfer in a relativistic plane–parallel flow has been reexamined under a non-gray treatment, while focusing our attention on the scattering effect. Under the assumption of a constant flow speed and using a variable Eddington factor, we analytically solved the relativistic transfer equations in the comoving frame for several cases, such as radiative equilibrium or local thermodynamical equilibrium, and obtained analytical solutions for the emergent intensity as well as other radiative quantities. In the case of the radiative equilibrium, the scattering effect does not appear, and the solutions are formally the same as those under the gray case, although the frequency-dependent intensity was obtained for the first time. In the case of local thermodynamic equilibrium, on the other hand, the scattering effect is significant in isothermal flow, similar to a static isothermal atmosphere. That is, the source function reduces near to the flow top, and the emergent intensity decreases toward the limb due to scattering. In both cases, when the flow optical depth becomes small, the emergent intensity toward the pole decreases due to the effect of a finite optical depth. In addition, the emergent intensity and other quantities in the fixed (inertial) frame are enhanced due to relativistic effects.

articleTitle: SGRs and AXPs as Rotation-Powered Massive White Dwarfs
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: SGR 0418<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>5729 is a “Rosetta Stone” for deciphering the energy source of Soft Gamma Ray Repeaters (SGRs) and Anomalous X-ray Pulsars (AXPs). We present a model based on canonical physics and astrophysics for SGRs and AXPs powered by massive highly magnetized rotating white dwarfs (WDs), in total analogy with pulsars powered by rotating neutron stars (NSs). We predict for SGR 0418<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>5729 a lower limit for its spin-down rate, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{P}~\geq~L_{\rm X} P^3/$</tex>(4<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pi^2 I$</tex>) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 1.18 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-16}$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$I$</tex> is the moment of inertia of the WD. We show for SGRs and AXPs that the occurrence of the glitch and the gain of rotational energy is due to the release of gravitational energy associated to the contraction and decrease of the moment of inertia of the WDs. The steady emission and the outburst following the glitch are explained by the loss of rotational energy of the WDs, in view of the much larger moment of inertia of the WDs, as compared to that of NSs and/or quark stars. There is no need here to invoke the unorthodox concept of magnetic energy release due to the decay of overcritical magnetic fields, as assumed in the magnetar model. A new astrophysical scenario for the SGRs and AXPs associated to Supernova remnants is presented. The observational campaigns of the X-ray Japanese satellite Suzaku on AE Aquarii and the corresponding theoretical works by Japanese groups and recent results of the Hubble Space Telescope, give crucial information for our theoretical model. Follow-on missions of Hubble Telescope and VLT are highly recommended to give further observational evidence of this most fundamental issue of relativistic astrophysics: the identification of the true SGRs/AXPs energy source.

Author Keywords: stars: massive fast rotating highly magnetized white dwarfs

articleTitle: Suzaku Investigation into the Nature of the Nearest Ultraluminous X-Ray Source, M33 X-8
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The X-ray spectrum of the nearest ultraluminous X-ray source, M 33 X-8, obtained by Suzaku during 2010 January 11–13, was closely analyzed in order to examine its nature. It is, by far, the only data with the highest signal statistic in the 0.4–10 keV range. Despite being able to reproduce the X-ray spectrum, Comptonization of the disk photons failed to give a physically meaningful solution. A modified version of the multi-color disk model, in which the dependence of the disk temperature on the radius is described as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ r^{-p}$</tex>, with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ p$</tex> being a free parameter, can also approximate the spectrum. From this model, the innermost disk temperature and bolometric luminosity were obtained as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ T_{\rm in}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 2.00<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ _{-0.05}^{+0.06}$</tex> keV and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ L_{\rm disk}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 1.36 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{39}$</tex> (cos <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ i$</tex> )<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex>, respectively, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ i$</tex> is the disk inclination. A small temperature gradient of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ p$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0.535<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ _-0.005^{+0.004}$</tex>, together with the high disk temperature, is regarded as signatures of the slim accretion disk model, suggesting that M 33 X-8 was accreting at a high mass-accretion rate. With a correction factor for the slim-disk taken into account, the innermost disk radius, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ R_{\rm in}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 81.9<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ _-6.5^{+5.9}$</tex> (cos<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ i$</tex> )<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-0.5}$</tex> km, corresponds to a black-hole mass of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ M$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 10 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ M_{\odot}$</tex> (cos <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ i$</tex> )<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-0.5}$</tex> . Accordingly, the bolometric disk luminosity is estimated to be about 80(cos <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ i$</tex> )<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-0.5}$</tex> % of the Eddington limit. A numerically calculated slim-disk spectrum was found to reach a similar result. Thus, the extremely super-Eddington luminosity is not required to explain the nature of M 33 X-8. This conclusion is utilized to argue for the existence of intermediate-mass black holes with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ M$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ >rsim$</tex> 100<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ M_{\odot}$</tex> radiating at the sub/trans-Eddington luminosity, among ultraluminous X-ray sources with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ L_{\rm disk}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ >rsim$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{40}$</tex> erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> .

articleTitle: Suzaku X-Ray Observation of the Dwarf Nova Z Camelopardalis at the Onset of an Optical Outburst
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the result of a Suzaku X-ray spectroscopic observation of the dwarf nova Z Cam, which was conducted by chance at the onset of an optical outburst. We used the X-ray Imaging Spectrometer (a 38 ks exposure) and the Hard X-ray Detector (34 ks) to obtain a 0.35–40 keV spectrum simultaneously. Spectral characteristics suggest that the source was in the X-ray quiescent state, despite being in the rising phase of an outburst in the optical band. The spectrum shows a clear signature of circumstellar absorption in excess of interstellar absorption and the reprocessed-emission features of Fe fluorescence and Compton scattering. The extra absorption is explained as being due to partial covering by either neutral or ionized matter. We found a spectral change during the observation, which is attributable only to a change in the circumstellar absorption. Such an X-ray spectral variation was reported for the first time in the case of dwarf novae. We speculate that the variation in the circumstellar absorption is interpreted as a time-varying disk wind, or geometrically flaring disk around the white dwarf during the propagation of a heat wave along inward the accretion disk at the beginning of the outburst, in which optical outburst and X-ray quiescent states co-exist.

articleTitle: A Planetary Companion to the Intermediate-Mass Giant HD 100655
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: A precise radial-velocity survey conducted by a Korean–Japanese planet search program revealed a planetary companion around the intermediate-mass clump giant HD 100655. The radial velocity of the star exhibits a periodic Keplerian variation with a period, semi-amplitude, and eccentricity of 157.57 d, 35.2 m s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, and 0.085, respectively. Adopting an estimated stellar mass of 2.4<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ M_{\odot}$</tex>, we confirmed the presence of a planetary companion with a semi-major axis of 0.76 AU and a minimum mass of 1.7<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ M_{\mathrm{J}}$</tex>. The planet is the lowest-mass planet yet discovered around clump giants with masses greater than 1.9<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ M_{\odot}$</tex>.

articleTitle: Lithium, Sodium, and Potassium Abundances in Sharp-Lined A-Type Stars
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The abundances of alkali elements (Li, Na, and K) were determined from the Li I 6708, Na I 5682/5688, and K I 7699 lines by taking into account the non-LTE effect for 24 sharp-lined A-type stars (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$v _{\rm e}$</tex> sin <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$i$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex> 50 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, 7000 K <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm eff}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex> 10000 K, many showing Am peculiarities to different degrees), based on high-dispersion and high-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$S/N$</tex> spectral data secured at BOAO (Korea) and OAO (Japan). We found a significant trend that <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A$</tex>(Na) tightly scales with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A$</tex>(Fe) irrespective of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm eff}$</tex>, which means that Na becomes enriched similarly to Fe in accordance with the degree of Am peculiarity. Regarding lithium, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A$</tex>(Li) mostly ranges between <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 3 and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 3.5 (i.e., almost the same as or slightly less than the solar system abundance of 3.3) with a weak decreasing tendency with a lowering of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm eff}$</tex> at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm eff}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex> 8000 K, though several stars exceptionally show distinctly larger depletion. The abundances of potassium also revealed an apparent <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm eff}$</tex>-dependence in the sense that <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A$</tex>(K) in late-A stars tends to be mildly subsolar [possibly with a weak anti-correlation with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A$</tex>(Fe)] systematically decreasing from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 5.0 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm eff}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 8500 K) to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 4.6 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm eff}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 7500 K), while those for early-A stars remain near-solar around <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 5.0–5.2. These observational facts may serve as important constraints for any theory aiming to explain chemical anomalies of A-type stars.

articleTitle: Orbital Period Investigation of the RS CVn-Type Binary CG Cygni
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We collected all minima times of the RS CVn-type binary CG Cyg that we were able to find in the literature and databases. The orbital period variations of the system were examined by analyzing its <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ O$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ C$</tex> curves (1) through the weighted least-squares method, and (2) through the first continuous method. It was found that the results obtained from the two methods are different. We compared our results with the former author's work, and drew the orbital-period variation of CG Cyg, which indicates that it undergoes a long-term period increase at a rate of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ dP/dt$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 2.48 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-8}$</tex> d yr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> . We discuss the implications of the result regarding the link between the orbital-period variation and the mass transfer of the system.

articleTitle: Constraining Intergalactic Magnetic Field with Fermi-LAT Observation of Cascade Radiation for TeV Blazars
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The problem concerning the origin of the Intergalactic Magnetic Field (IGMF) is one of the long-standing problems of astrophysics and cosmology, and direct measurements are difficult. TeV photons emitted by TeV blazars produce electron-positron pairs because of interactions with the extragalactic background light (EBL). These pairs emit secondary cascade gamma-rays via Inverse Compton scattering of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) photons. In this process, the trajectories of the pairs are deviated by the IGMF, and the cascade gamma-ray emission appears as extended emission around TeV source. We used the EBL, synchrotron self-Compton (SSC) model and the observed limits on Lorentz factor of electron-positron pairs to calculate the cascade-radiation spectrum, and then to fit the observed GeV to TeV and multi-waveband spectra of TeV blazars to constrain the IGMF. We obtained the GeV energy spectra of three TeV blazars by analyzing the Fermi-LAT data of the past <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim$</tex> 3 yr. The flux upper limits of Fermi-LAT in the 90% significant level of 1ES 0229<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 200 suggests that the IGMF is stronger than 2 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-18}$</tex> G for an engine time of TeV activity with three years. The relationships between the deduced lower limits of IGMF and various engine times for 1ES 0229<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 200 and 1ES 0347<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 121 are presented by us.

articleTitle: Non-Equilibrium Ionization State and Two-Temperature Structure in the Bullet Cluster 1E 0657−56
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We investigate a non-equilibrium ionization state and an electron–ion two-temperature structure of the intracluster medium in the merging galaxy cluster, 1E 0657<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>56 (Bullet cluster), using a series of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N$</tex>-body and hydrodynamic simulations. We find that the electron temperature at the shock layer associated with the X-ray sub-peak (bullet) is quite different depending on the thermal relaxation model between electrons and ions; <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>25 keV for the Coulomb thermal relaxation model and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>45 keV for the instantaneous thermal relaxation model in the simulations which reproduce the observed X-ray morphology. Furthermore, both of Fe XXV and Fe XXVI are overabundant compared with the ionization equilibrium state around the shock layer, and thus, the intensity ratio between Fe XXV and Fe XXVI K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> lines are significantly altered from that in the ionization equilibrium state. We also carry out the simulations with various sets of merger parameters, and discuss a possible range of the non-equilibrium effects in this system. Our results could be tested with future X-ray observations such as Astro-H with better sensitivity in high energy band.

articleTitle: A Method of Identifying AGNs Based on Emission-Line Excess and the Nature of Low-Luminosity AGNs in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. I. A New Method
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We developed a new technique for identifying active galactic nuclei (AGNs) and studied the nature of low-luminosity AGNs in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. This is the former part of a series of papers. We develop a new, sensitive method of identifying AGNs in this paper. The emission-line luminosity in a spectrum is the sum of a star-formation component and an AGN component (if present). We demonstrate that an accurate estimate of the star-formation component can be achieved by fitting model spectra, generated with a recent stellar population synthesis code, to a continuum spectrum. By comparing the observed total line luminosity with that attributed to star formation, we can tell whether a galaxy hosts an AGN or not. We compare our method with the commonly used emission-line diagnostics proposed by Baldwin, Phillips, and Terlevich (1981, PASP, 93, 5; hereafter BPT). By this method, we classify 85% of the strong emission-line objects in the same star-formation/AGN as BPT. One unique feature of our method is its sensitivity; it is applicable to nearly twice as many objects as BPT. We further make a comparison between our method and the BPT diagnostics using stacked spectra and selections in X-ray and radio wavelengths. We show that it is overall a sensitive method of identifying AGNs, while our method suffers from incompleteness and contamination as any AGN identification method does so. We emphasize that our method can be applied at high redshifts (up to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${z}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 1.7 with red-sensitive optical spectrograph) without making any a priori assumptions about the host-galaxy properties. Another unique feature is that it allows us to subtract the emission-line luminosity due to star formation, and to extract the intrinsic AGN luminosity.

articleTitle: Tidal-Force-Induced Precessions of Accretion Disks
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The preccession of an accretion disk around a compact star in a close binary has been studied. When the accretion disk tilts, the tidal force from the companion star induces a torque on it, which causes a preccession of the disk. We firstly consider the properties of a preccessing motion of a ring, which is circularly rotating around a compact star, and is preccessing with a slightly tilting angle under the influence of a tidal force from a companion star. We next compare the predicted behaviors of the preccessing ring with observations, and find that several observational facts from Her X-1, SS 433, and some other X-ray binaries can be explained by a tidal-force-induced precession scheme quite reasonably. We further examine the energetics of the preccessing ring as a function of the tilting angle. It is shown that the kinetic and potential energies of the orbiting motions of the ring matter around the compact star increases as the tilting angle increases, while the thermal and effective potential energies for hydro-static balance in the meridian cross section of the ring decreases through adiabatic expansion. Quantitative estimations have shown that when the ring has sufficient thermal energy, the decrease of the energy for the hydro-static balance can be larger than the increase of the energy for circular motion around the compact star until the tilting angle reaches a certain value. It is strongly suggested that preccessions of accretion disks are often realized in close binaries.

articleTitle: Water-Vapor Maser Disk at the Nucleus of the Seyfert 2 Galaxy IC 2560 and its Distance
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the results of single-dish and VLBI observations for the water-vapor masers at the nucleus of a Seyfert 2, IC 2560. We monitored the velocities of the maser features with the 45-m telescope of the Nobeyama Radio Observatory. Using data form 1995–2006, the velocity drift rate was detected to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \bar{a}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 2.57 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm$</tex> 0.04 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> yr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-1}$</tex> on the average for 6 systemic features. The Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) with the Very Large Array (VLA) firstly detected red-shifted and blue-shifted maser features of IC 2560, in addition to systemic maser features and a continuum component. We propose a maser disk in the nuclear region. The systemic and red-shifted features are emitted from a nearly edge-on disk with a position angle of PA<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> 46<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{\circ}$</tex>, which is almost perpendicular to the galactic disk. Assuming Keplerian rotation, the radii of the maser disk are <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ r$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0.087–0.335 pc, and the thickness is 2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ H$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \leq$</tex> 0.025 pc. The binding mass is 3.5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{6}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ M\odot$</tex> at a distance of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ D$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 26 Mpc, and the mean volume density within the inner radius is 1.3 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{9}M\odot$</tex> pc<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{-3}$</tex>, strongly suggesting a massive black hole at the center. A continuum component was detected at 0.2 pc southwest of the disk center, and is considered to be a jet ejected from the nucleus, with an angle of 70<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{\circ}$</tex> from the disk. The blue-shifted maser feature is located on the continuum component, being interpreted to be a ``jet maser.'' The distance to IC 2560 was estimated to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ D$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 31<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{+12}_{-14}$</tex> Mpc from the geometry of the maser disk and the velocity drift rate.

articleTitle: NIR Spectroscopy of Star-Forming Galaxies at z ∼ 1.4 with Subaru/FMOS: The Mass–Metallicity Relation
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present near-infrared spectroscopic observations of star-forming galaxies at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex> 1.4 with FMOS on the Subaru Telescope. We observed <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K$</tex>-band selected galaxies in the SXDS/UDS fields with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\leq$</tex> 23.9 mag, 1.2 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\leq$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z_{\rm ph}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\leq$</tex> 1.6, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{*}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\geq$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{9.5}\ M_{\odot}$</tex>, and expected F(H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex>) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\geq$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-16}\ $</tex>erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}\ $</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex>; 71 objects in the sample have significant detections of H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex>. For these objects, excluding possible AGNs, identified from the BPT diagram, gas-phase metallicities were obtained from the [N II] / H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> line ratio. The sample is split into three stellar-mass bins, and the spectra are stacked in each stellar-mass bin. The mass–metallicity relation obtained at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex> 1.4 is located between those at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex> 0.8 and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex> 2.2. We constrain the intrinsic scatter to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex> 0.1 dex, or larger in the mass–metallicity relation at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex> 1.4; the scatter may be larger at higher redshifts. We found trends that the deviation from the mass–metallicity relation depends on the SFR (Star-formation rate) and the half light radius: Galaxies with higher SFR and larger half light radii show lower metallicities at a given stellar mass. One possible scenario for the trends is the infall of pristine gas accreted from IGM, or through merger events. Our data points show larger scatter than the fundamental metallicity relation (FMR) at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex> 0.1, and the average metallicities slightly deviate from the FMR. The compilation of the mass–metallicity relations at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex> 3 to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex> 0.1 shows that they evolve smoothly from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex> 3 to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex> 0 without changing the shape so much, except for the massive part at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex> 0.

articleTitle: Search for X-Ray Emission Associated with the Shapley Supercluster with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Suzaku performed observations of 3 regions in and around the Shapley supercluster, a region located between A 3558 and A 3556, at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>0.9 times the virial radii of both clusters, and two other regions at 1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ$</tex> and 4<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ$</tex> away from the first pointing. The 4<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ$</tex>-offset observation was used to evaluate the Galactic foreground emission. We did not detect significant redshifted Oxygen emission lines (O VII and O VIII) in the spectra of all three pointings, after subtracting the contribution of foreground and background emission. The upper limit for the redshifted O VIII K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> line intensity of the warm-hot intergalactic medium (WHIM) is 1.5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-7}$</tex> photons s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex> arcmin<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex>, which corresponds to an overdensity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>380 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$Z/$</tex>0.1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ Z_{\odot}$</tex>)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1/2}$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L/$</tex>3 Mpc)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1/2}$</tex>, assuming <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 3 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{6}$</tex> K. We found excess continuum emission in the 1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ$</tex>-offset and on-filament regions, represented by thermal models with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ kT\sim 1$</tex> keV and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>2 keV, respectively. The redshifts of both 0 and that of the supercluster (0.048) are consistent with the observed spectra. The <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>1 keV emission can also be fitted with Ne-rich Galactic (zero redshift) thin thermal emission. The radial intensity profile of the 2 keV component suggests contributions from A 3558 and A 3556, but with significant steepening of the intensity slope in the outer region of A 3558. Finally, we summarized the previous Suzaku search for the WHIM, and discussed the feasibility of constraining the WHIM. An overdensity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$<\ $</tex>400 could be detectable using O VII and O VIII emission lines in a range of 1.4 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{6}$</tex> K <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$<\ $</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$<\ $</tex> 5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{6}$</tex> K or a continuum emission in a relatively high-temperature range of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>$</tex> 5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{6}$</tex> K with the Suzaku XIS. The non-detection with Suzaku suggests that a typical line-of-sight average overdensity is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$<\ $</tex>400.

articleTitle: The 3 mm Spectral Line Survey toward the Lynds 1157 B1 Shocked Region. I. Data
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have conducted a spectral line survey of the 3 mm band with the 45 m telescope of Nobeyama Radio Observatory toward the L 1157 B1 shocked region, where the blue-shifted component of the bipolar outflow from the protostar IRAS 20386<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ +$</tex> 6751 interacts with the ambient gas. The observed frequency ranges from 78.1 to 115.8 GHz. We have detected 129 spectral lines of 29 molecular species. In addition to various oxygen-bearing organic molecules such as CH<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ _3$</tex> CHO, HCOOCH<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ _3$</tex>, and HCOOH, we have detected a phosphorus-containing molecule PN, a nitrogen-bearing organic molecule NH<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ _2$</tex> CHO, and a carbon-chain molecule CCS in the shocked region. These results clearly indicate that the L 1157 B1 shocked region is chemically rich, which is probably triggered by evaporation of grain mantles.

articleTitle: An Attempt to Describe Frequency Correlations among kHz QPOs and HBOs by Two-Armed Nearly Vertical Oscillations
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We examine whether the two-armed (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$m$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 2) vertical p-mode oscillations trapped in the innermost region of magnetized accretion disks with finite disk thickness can describe kHz quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) and horizontal branch oscillations (HBOs) in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs). First, we derive the frequency–frequency correlation of the two basic oscillations (both are fundamental modes in the vertical direction, but one is the fundamental and the other the first overtone in the radial direction), and compare it with the observed frequency correlation of twin kHz QPOs. Results show that the calculated frequency correlation can well describe the observed frequency one with reasonable values of the parameters. Second, we examine whether the observed frequency correlation between kHz QPOs and HBO can be described by regarding HBO as the first overtone oscillation in the vertical direction (and the fundamental in the radial direction). The results suggest that (i) the innermost parts of disks on the horizontal branch are strongly diminished in their vertical thickness (presumably by hot coronae) and (ii) the branch is roughly a sequence of variations of magnetic fields or disk temperature.

articleTitle: V369 Gem: A New Ellipsoidal Variable System with High-level Chromospheric Activity
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In this study, we present BVR photometry of V369 Gem in 2006–2008. We combined our <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V$</tex> data with the data taken from the literature. We analysed all of the data together, and calculated new light elements. General features of the light curves were discussed. The light curves were modelled with the Fourier method, and the Fourier coefficients were calculated. The cos (2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \theta$</tex> ) term was found to be dominant. The pre-whitened <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V$</tex> light curves demonstrated that stellar spot activity also exists. There are generally two minima in the pre-whitened light curves. Thus, there must be two spotted areas, which are separated by about 180<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{\circ}$</tex> from each other. As conclusions, we have remarked for the first time that V369 Gem is an ellipsoidal variable with high-level chromospheric activity.

articleTitle: An Attempt to Describe Frequency-Correlations among kHz QPOs and HBOs by Two-Armed Vertical p-Mode Oscillations: Case of No Magnetic Field
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The trapping of two-armed (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ m$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 2) vertical p-mode oscillations in relativistic disks is examined. The disks are assumed to be isothermal in the vertical direction, but are truncated at a certain height by the presence of corona. The same issues were examined in a previous paper (Kato 2012a). In this paper, unlike the previous paper, however, we do not use the approximation that the oscillations are nearly vertical, but limit to a simpler case of no magnetic field. As in the previous paper, the results suggest that the two basic oscillation modes [both are the fundamental (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ n$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 1) in the vertical direction, but in the horizontal direction one is the fundamental (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ n_{\rm r}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0) and the other the first overtone (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ n_{\rm r}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 1)] correspond to the twin kHz QPOs. Second, the oscillation mode, which is the first overtone (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ n$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 2) in the vertical direction and the fundamental in the horizontal direction (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ n_{\rm r}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ =$</tex> 0), will correspond to the horizontal branch oscillation (HBO) of Z-sources. The latter suggests that the horizontal branch of Z-sources is a sequence of temperature change in disks whose vertical thickness is strongly terminated. The temperature increases leftward along the sequence from the apex between the normal and horizontal branches.

articleTitle: Suzaku Observation of Nearby On-Going Merger Cluster Abell 3627
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the results of the Suzaku observation of a nearby (z <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 0.016), on-going merger cluster, Abell 3627.
